searchDocs.title: What changed since the first beta​
searchDocs.content: When I announced the beta in September, I said it held more than a version bump. The betas since then have made the packages behave the way modern tooling expects. They also fixed the places where the charts said one thing and did another. Here is what you will notice:  One bundle per package, built with Vite. Version 2 published a file for every chart. Version 3 now publishes one UMD bundle and one CDN bundle per package, plus ES modules for bundlers. Bundlers already drop the charts you do not import, so a file per chart saved nothing there. On a page with a script tag, one request is better than five.Real ES module packages. The three packages declare "type": "module", so import works in Node as well as in bundlers, with matching types for each way of loading. require still works and loads the CommonJS bundle, which now ends in .cjs.Charts that screen readers can name. Every chart gives its svg a role and an accessible name, "Bar chart" by default. Set a11yTitle to name it after what it shows. Set a11yDescription to add a sentence about what it means.Negative values in the scatter plot. Its value axis now runs below zero when the data does, and each circle's size shows the size of its value. That completes the negative values work: the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts all draw them.Typings that match the charts. I compared every chart's published types with what it does at run time, and fixed more than a hundred mismatches. Getters were declared as setters, callbacks had the wrong return type, and accessors were declared but never existed. If TypeScript accepts a call now, the chart does what the call says.Smaller fixes you may have hit. The brush honours locale and the stacked area honours numberFormat, which both used to do nothing. The scatter plot's zoom works again. The grouped and stacked bar tooltips no longer flicker when you move across the bars. Resting the pointer on a chart no longer pops up the browser's own tooltip. A chart's valueLocale no longer changes the numbers of every other chart on the page. A colorMap that names only some categories colours the rest from the palette.Tooltips that say what each chart needs. The charts name the fields of the data they send the tooltip differently. Some of them need the tooltip told where to look: topicLabel('values') for the stacked area, nameLabel('stack') or nameLabel('group') for the stacked and grouped bars, valueLabel('y') for the scatter plot. The tooltip reference and a new how-to list them per chart. Every story shows them in use.Leaner API pages and more recipes. Each accessor's heading starts with its name instead of exports., in the pages and in their tables of contents. The how-to guides gain recipes for per-category colours, number and date formats, loading states, animation, negative values and accessibility.In React, Tooltip infers its data type from its data prop, so its render callback type-checks without a cast. Seven settings the charts always had are now props, and prop-types is no longer a peer dependency.

searchDocs.title: What to check before you upgrade​
searchDocs.content: If you tried an earlier beta, five changes in this stretch can break your code. The migration guide covers each of them with a before and after:  Per-chart files are gone. Import the charts from the package, or load dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js and use the core global.CommonJS bundles end in .cjs. This matters only if you required a bundle by its path.The bullet chart and the sparkline no longer draw titles. Text inside an svg cannot wrap and ignores your page's typography, so put the label in your own markup and pass the same text to a11yTitle.An accessor you have not set reads null, on every chart. Before, some charts returned undefined. A truthiness check works as before.The data-key accessors are gone. nameLabel, valueLabel, dateLabel and the rest no longer let a chart read your data under other keys. They had warned since version 2 that they would go. Rename the keys in your data to the ones the chart's data shape names, such as name and value. The tooltip keeps its own four.  If you are coming from version 2, the guide has the full list. Version 2 ends at 2.18.2.

searchDocs.title: What happens next​
searchDocs.content: Between now and 3.0.0, I only plan to fix bugs. The API is settled, so if something in it is wrong, now is the last cheap moment to say so. After 3.0.0 ships, changing it means another major version.  So please try this beta in a real project. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected. The Storybook shows every chart and its options, in core and in React. It is the fastest way to check whether something is a bug or a setting.  Britecharts still needs maintainers. If you would like to own part of it, the contributing guide is where to start.

searchDocs.title: Why there is another beta​
searchDocs.content: I wrote that beta 7 would be the last beta, and that only bug fixes would come before 3.0.0. That did not happen. I compared Britecharts with eight current charting libraries, and the comparison showed what Britecharts can do better than any of them: finished charts that are accessible by default, free, and easy for an agent to write. Most of that work changes the API, so it had to land before 3.0.0 fixes the API in place.

searchDocs.title: Accessible by default​
searchDocs.content: Only one library in that comparison gave readers a data table, keyboard navigation and reduced motion together, and it charges per seat. Every Britecharts chart now does all of it, with each part on by default and each one possible to turn off. See how to make a chart accessible.  Its data as a table. Every chart but the legend renders its data as a visually hidden table after its svg, so a screen reader can read it cell by cell. Series charts lay it out with a row per date or name and a column per series. Turn it off with a11yDataTable(false).A keyboard can move through the data. The bar, donut, grouped bar, heatmap, line, scatter plot, stacked area and stacked bar charts are each one tab stop. The arrow keys move between points, Home and End go to the ends, and Escape lets go. The point is highlighted and the tooltip follows focus, as they do for a pointer. Turn it off with a11yKeyboardNavigation(false).Still when the reader asks. With prefers-reduced-motion, the charts draw without animation whatever isAnimated says, and the tooltip and legend stop fading.A colour-blind-safe palette. colors.colorSchemas.okabeIto keeps its eight colours apart with the common kinds of colour blindness.

searchDocs.title: Themes and dark mode, with CSS​
searchDocs.content: Every colour around the data is now a --bc-* custom property: text, axes, grid, tooltips, legend and loading states. The charts follow your page's color-scheme through light-dark(), so color-scheme: light dark on your page is all dark mode needs. To change one colour, set its token, such as .britechart { --bc-text-muted: #555 }. A page that declares no colour scheme stays light. See how to theme a chart.

searchDocs.title: Made for coding agents​
searchDocs.content: An agent writes a chart correctly more often when the library tells it what it needs. This beta adds four ways to do that:  An agent skill ships in @britecharts/core, with each chart's data shape, accessors, events and the v2 code that no longer works. Install it with npx skills add britecharts/britecharts.A JSON Schema for every chart's spec, { chart, config, data }, generated from the TypeScript types and published at https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/<chart>.json. An editor or an agent can check a spec before drawing it. See how to describe a chart as a spec.Errors that say how to fix them. A misspelt key gets heigth: did you mean height? and a link to the chart's API page. A value of the wrong type names the type it should be.llms.txt describes every chart and accessor, generated from the same comments as the API pages.

searchDocs.title: New in the charts​
searchDocs.content: 100% stacks. isNormalized(true) stretches every stack of the stacked bar, or every date of the stacked area, to fill the value axis, which then reads from 0% to 100%.Any categories in the heatmap. xAxisLabels joins yAxisLabels, so a heatmap can compare any two sets of categories, such as a square grid of six.SVG export. exportChart('chart.svg') downloads an svg with its styles inlined, so it looks the same outside the page and stays sharp at any size.Every chart in every package. The brush and the heatmap now have a wrapper and a React component, like the other charts.Fixes you may have hit. The brush no longer flickers on a second selection or fires customBrushEnd while idle. The animated stacked bar grows each stack as one block. The legend's highlight commands no longer throw before it draws. A bullet can have more than one marker.Smaller app bundles. Each package declares sideEffects, so bundlers can drop the charts an app does not import. In a bar-only test app, the bundle went from 104.0 kB to 89.6 kB.    The Storybook shows all of it, with the same stories under the same names in core and in React.

searchDocs.title: What to check before you upgrade​
searchDocs.content: Five changes in this beta can affect a page that works with beta 7:  Charts add a tab stop and a hidden table. If your page has its own table of the same data, or a tab order to keep, turn them off with a11yDataTable(false) or a11yKeyboardNavigation(false).The wrappers check value types. create and update throw on a value of the wrong type, such as height: "300". Before, the string reached the chart.An exported title gets its own band. The title sits in a 30px band above the chart instead of over its top edge, so an exported image with a title is 30px taller.The heatmap's label classes changed. .day-label is now .row-label, .hour-label is .column-label, and their groups are .row-labels-group and .column-labels-group. The row labels now end at the grid, and both axes share one label style.Some colours are set as styles now. The tooltip's text, the donut's empty slice, the scatter plot's hollow circles, the line chart's custom lines, the sparkline's gradient and the heatmap's labels take their colours from the --bc-* tokens, set on the element. A CSS rule on those elements no longer wins, so set the token instead.  If you are coming from version 2, the migration guide has the full list.

searchDocs.title: What happens next​
searchDocs.content: The API work I wanted before 3.0.0 is done, so this time I mean it: what follows is bug fixes, then 3.0.0. Bigger features, such as server-side rendering, a Canvas renderer or Web Component bindings, wait as issues that need votes. Add a 👍 to the ones you would use.  Please try this beta in a real project, with a screen reader and a keyboard if you can. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected.  Britecharts still needs maintainers. If you would like to own part of it, the contributing guide is where to start.

searchDocs.title: What is new​
searchDocs.content: There is more here than a version bump, so let me go through it in the order I think you will actually notice it:  Modern modules. Built on the current d3 modules, shipped as ES modules, CommonJS, UMD and CDN builds, with an exports map and TypeScript typings for every chart. Vite, Rollup, esbuild and webpack all work out of the box, which was not true of v2 — every bundler had its own workaround, and I was tired of maintaining them.Smaller bundles. The build now targets ES2020, and Babel is gone entirely from @britecharts/core and @britecharts/wrappers — the core UMD bundle drops 12.7% (151,923 → 132,626 bytes) and the React bundle 14% (368 → 315 KB). You do not need to do anything for this one; a browser below the new target already needs a bundler or its own polyfills to run modern syntax at all, so nothing that worked before stops working now.One tooltip. tooltip and miniTooltip used to be two components with two sets of bugs. They are one now, and it never gets cut off at the chart's edges, follows the pointer smoothly, and behaves the same way whichever chart it is attached to.Negative values on the bar, stacked bar, grouped bar and brush charts, stacking down from zero. This has been the second-most-requested thing since 2019, and the reason it took this long is that I kept underestimating how much of the domain math assumed zero was the floor.Loading states for every chart, colorMap to name the colour of each category, animationDuration on every animated chart, and charts that are responsive by default.React 19 is tested end to end, not just claimed: the unit suite itself now runs on React 19, and the React package is also installed into a real React 19 project under StrictMode on every change. If you have been holding off upgrading because you weren't sure the wrappers would survive StrictMode's double-invoked effects, that is exactly what this checks.

searchDocs.title: Moving from version 2​
searchDocs.content: Most of the work is renaming, and I tried to keep it that way on purpose — a rewrite nobody can follow is worse than a major version nobody wants to install. The migration guide walks through every breaking change with a before and after for each. The ones you will hit first:  Imports. The charts are named exports of @britecharts/core (import { bar } from '@britecharts/core') instead of files under britecharts/dist/umd. The CommonJS, UMD and CDN paths are in the guide too.Loading states. loadingState() is gone; render the chart with isLoading(true) and a dataset, empty or not.Renamed accessors. locale is valueLocale on the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot; the value formatters of the grouped and stacked bar are numberFormat; the line and stacked area swap xAxisFormat and xAxisCustomFormat back to what their names say; aspectRatio is removed.Tooltips. The line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts now dispatch customMouseMove the same way every other chart does, as (dataPoint, [x, y], [width, height], colorMap). If you drive tooltip.update yourself, it still accepts the old argument order and warns once.exportChart returns a promise.  Version 2 ends at 2.18.2. I am not going to pretend I will keep patching it once 3.0 ships, so if you are on v2 and this list looks manageable, better to do it now than after a security report forces the question.

searchDocs.title: Where to start​
searchDocs.content: The installation and getting started tutorials build a first chart from scratch, and styling charts covers themes and CSS.The API reference has a page per chart and one for the tooltip.The Storybook shows every chart, in core and in React, with its options live — that is usually faster than reading accessor names off a page.

searchDocs.title: Tell us what breaks​
searchDocs.content: A beta is only useful if people actually try to break it, so please do. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected instead — the more specific, the faster I can act on it.  I will also say plainly what the contributing guide says: Britecharts needs maintainers. I have carried this release mostly on my own, and a 3.7k-star library with one person behind it is not a sustainable place to leave it. If any part of this codebase is something you would enjoy owning, that guide is where to start the conversation.

searchDocs.title: Try it​
searchDocs.content: Press Tab until a chart has focus, then use the arrow keys. With a screen reader, move past a chart to reach its table.  Uses of each word Uses over a week  Key	DoesRight or Left arrow	moves to the next or previous data point: a bar, a slice, a date, a point Down or Up arrow	the same, except on the heatmap, where they move a day Home, End	moves to the first or last point Escape	lets go of the point; leaving the chart does too

searchDocs.title: Name each chart​
searchDocs.content: The default name says what kind of chart it is, not what it shows. Name it after its data, and add a sentence about what it means:  barChart .a11yTitle('Monthly visits') .a11yDescription('Visits doubled in May');   In React, pass a11yTitle and a11yDescription as props. The data table takes the chart's name as its caption.

searchDocs.title: What each chart supports​
searchDocs.content: Chart	Name and description	Data table	KeyboardBar, grouped bar, stacked bar	yes	yes	yes Line, stacked area	yes	yes	yes Donut, heatmap, scatter plot, treemap	yes	yes	yes Brush, bullet, sparkline	yes	yes	no Legend	yes	no	no  The bullet chart and the sparkline draw no title. Put their label in your own markup, next to the chart, and give screen readers the same words with a11yTitle.

searchDocs.title: How other libraries compare​
searchDocs.content: What each library does by default, from its own documentation, as of October 2026:  	Britecharts	Highcharts	Recharts	Chart.jsName for screen readers	on by default	with the accessibility module	on by default since 3.0	you add aria-label and role to the canvas Data as a table	on by default, hidden	with the export-data module	no	no; you write fallback content Keyboard through the data	on by default, 8 charts	with the accessibility module	on by default since 3.0	no Sonification	no	yes	no	no Frameworks	plain JavaScript, React	plain JavaScript, official React, Angular, Vue and others	React	plain JavaScript, community wrappers License	Apache 2.0, free	commercial, from 366 USD per developer seat	MIT, free	MIT, free  Highcharts goes further than Britecharts. It adds sonification and more ways to read a chart, and every license includes its accessibility module. Britecharts is the free library in this table that gives screen readers both a name and a data table by default. It also gives keyboards a way through the data.  Sources: Highcharts accessibility module, Highcharts shop, Recharts 3.0 migration guide, Recharts and accessibility, Chart.js accessibility. See also Britecharts vs Chart.js, vs Recharts and vs Highcharts.

searchDocs.title: Turn a feature off​
searchDocs.content: Each feature is on by default and has an opt-out, for pages that already provide the same thing:  To turn off	Core	React	WrappersThe data table	.a11yDataTable(false)	a11yDataTable={false}	a11yDataTable: false Keyboard navigation	.a11yKeyboardNavigation(false)	a11yKeyboardNavigation={false}	a11yKeyboardNavigation: false  If the page already shows the same data in an accessible form, turn off the table. If charts are thumbnails in a list, turn off keyboard navigation so they don't each take a tab stop.

searchDocs.title: How it is tested​
searchDocs.content: Unit tests check the svg's role and name and each chart's table. Playwright tests run in real apps that install the packed packages. They read the data tables the way a screen reader finds them and press the keys to move the tooltip.  If something doesn't work with your screen reader or keyboard, open an issue and say which reader and browser you use.

searchDocs.title: The data​
searchDocs.content: The data is a single object, not an array:  Field	What it draws	Typical useranges	Full-height background bands, widest at the back and fading by opacity	Poor, fair and good thresholds measures	Thinner bars on top of the bands	The actual value, and optionally a second one such as a forecast markers	Vertical lines, optional	The target  Give the values in any order: the chart sorts them. The narrowest measure is the strongest, so a second, longer measure reads as a forecast. The axis runs from 0 to the largest value in any of the three fields, and the first three colours of colorSchema go to the ranges, the measures and the markers, in that order.

searchDocs.title: What it does not have​
searchDocs.content: The chart draws no label, so put the metric's name in your own markup next to it; a11yTitle only names it for screen readers. It has no tooltip and fires no events. searchDocs.title: Scale~AxisScale : function​
searchDocs.content: What a chart calls on an axis scale, typed structurally rather than as a d3 scale class.  Several charts hold two different kinds of scale in one variable: xScale is a scaleLinear when the chart is horizontal and a scaleBand when it is vertical, and yScale is the mirror image. No single d3 class describes either, and the isHorizontal flag cannot narrow a module-level let.GridScale in grid.ts and getBaselineExtent's scale parameter in domain.ts already type scales this way, for the same reason -- narrower about what is required, wider about what satisfies it. searchDocs.title: Reading each chart's data point​
searchDocs.content: The charts do not all name the fields of the data point they dispatch the same way, so the tooltip has to be told where to look for some of them. Without these settings, a tooltip on these charts shows no rows, rows without their colours, or no value:  Chart	Configure the tooltip with	Whyline	nothing	its data point carries date and topics, the defaults stacked area	topicLabel('values')	its rows are under values stacked bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('stack')	its rows are under values, named by stack grouped bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('group')	its rows are under values, named by group scatter plot	valueLabel('y')	a point's value is its y (add nameLabel('x') to show x instead of its name) bar, donut, heatmap, treemap	nothing	their data points carry name and value  In React, Tooltip starts from topicLabel('values'), so the line chart is the one that needs a setting there: topicLabel="topics".  Example  import { line, tooltip } from '@britecharts/core'; // dataset: { data: [{ topicName, name, date, value }] } line() .width(500) .tooltip(tooltip().title('Visits')) .render('.css-selector', dataset);   Tooltip tooltip(_selection, _data) .axisTimeCombinations.dateFormat(_x) ⇒ String | module.dateCustomFormat(_x) ⇒ String | module.dateLabel(_x) ⇒ String | module.hide() ⇒ module.locale(_x) ⇒ String | module.nameLabel(_x) ⇒ String | module.numberFormat(_x) ⇒ string | module.valueFormatter(_x) ⇒ function | module.shouldShowDateInTitle(_x) ⇒ Boolean | module.show([dataPoint], [position]) ⇒ module.title(_x) ⇒ String | module.tooltipOffset(_x) ⇒ Object | module.layout([_x]) ⇒ String | module.maxEntries([_x]) ⇒ Number | module.topicsOrder(_x) ⇒ Array.<String> | module.topicLabel(_x) ⇒ String | module.update(dataPoint, position, [chartSize], [colorMap]) ⇒ module.valueLabel(_x) ⇒ String | module.xAxisValueType([_x]) ⇒ String | module

searchDocs.title: Finished charts, not a grammar​
searchDocs.content: Grammar libraries hand you scales, marks and axes to assemble. Britecharts hands you a bar chart. Every chart shares one vocabulary (width, colorSchema, isLoading, numberFormat, exportChart, a11yTitle) and comes with loading and empty states, animation, tooltips and export already built. There are fewer ways to go wrong, for people and for coding agents alike.

searchDocs.title: Accessible by default, and free​
searchDocs.content: Every chart is accessible without any setup:  🔊 Named for screen readers, with its data as a table they can read cell by cell.⌨️ Keyboard navigable: tab to a chart, move between data points with the arrow keys, and the tooltip follows focus.🎞 Still when the reader asks for reduced motion.🎨 A colour-blind-safe palette, Okabe–Ito, one setting away.  Commercial libraries charge per seat for this set. In Britecharts it is on by default, and each part can be turned off.

searchDocs.title: One script tag or one config, in any page​
searchDocs.content: The vanilla core runs anywhere: a server-rendered template, a static site, a Web Component, or an AI sandbox that only allows CDN scripts. The same chart is available as a framework-agnostic wrapper and as a React component. And because a chart is a name, a configuration and data, it can be written down as a JSON spec that a schema checks before it's drawn.

searchDocs.title: Made for coding agents too​
searchDocs.content: Agents write Britecharts correctly on the first try more often when the library helps them:  📄 llms.txt and llms-full.txt describe every chart and accessor.🧠 An agent skill ships inside @britecharts/core, with each chart's data shape, accessors and common traps.✅ A JSON Schema for every chart's spec, so an editor or an agent can validate a config without running it.💬 Errors that say how to fix them: a misspelt key gets "did you mean height?" and a link to the chart's API page, and a value of the wrong type says what it should be.

searchDocs.title: Charting since 2015​
searchDocs.content: Britecharts started at Eventbrite in May 2015. Version 1 reached npm in March 2017, and version 2 followed that August. Since then, 55 people have contributed code and the repository has earned over 3,700 stars on GitHub. Version 2 is still installed about 5,000 times a week.  Version 3 keeps the idea that made those charts last: a chart is a function you configure and then call on your data. It rebuilds everything around it in TypeScript, with accessibility, theming, React components and tools for coding agents.

searchDocs.title: What's New in Version 3​
searchDocs.content: Version 3 is a rewrite of Britecharts in TypeScript, on D3 v7, as three packages: @britecharts/core, @britecharts/wrappers and @britecharts/react.  Accessibility built in. Named charts, data tables and keyboard navigation, reduced motion and the Okabe–Ito palette, all on by default.Theming and dark mode with standard CSS. Every colour around the data is a --bc-* custom property, and the charts follow the page's color-scheme through light-dark().Export to SVG or PNG from one call: exportChart('chart.svg').Chart specs and JSON Schemas, generated from the TypeScript types, with value checks in the wrappers.TypeScript types for every chart's data, configuration and React props.Every chart in every package, the brush and heatmap included, and one tooltip for all of them.Responsive by default: every svg scales to fit its container, with no resize listeners.Negative values in the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts, and loading states on every chart.Smaller bundles: ES modules that tree-shake, so an app only ships the charts it imports.  Coming from version 2? Read the migration guide.

searchDocs.title: Try it in your browser​
searchDocs.content: Open a running example on StackBlitz, in plain JavaScript or React, with nothing to install. Each draws a bar chart and a line chart with their tooltips, switches to dark mode, and moves through the data with the keyboard.

searchDocs.title: From a CDN, with no build step​
searchDocs.content: <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css" /> <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"></script> <div class="bar-container"></div> <script> core.bar() .height(300) .a11yTitle('Signups by plan') .tooltip(core.tooltip()) .render('.bar-container', [ { name: 'Pro', value: 412 }, { name: 'Team', value: 236 }, { name: 'Free', value: 1200 }, ]); </script>   The bundle includes d3, so the page needs no other script.

searchDocs.title: From npm​
searchDocs.content: npm install @britecharts/core   import { bar, tooltip } from '@britecharts/core'; import '@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css'; bar() .isHorizontal(true) .height(300) .a11yTitle('Signups by plan') .tooltip(tooltip()) .render('.bar-container', data);   render takes a CSS selector, an element or a d3 selection, and draws again with new data when you call it again. If you already use d3, select('.bar-container').datum(data).call(barChart) works too.

searchDocs.title: With React​
searchDocs.content: npm install @britecharts/react   import { Bar } from '@britecharts/react'; <Bar data={data} isHorizontal a11yTitle="Signups by plan" />;   In an app set up with shadcn/ui, one command adds a chart that follows your theme and its dark mode, with one registry item per chart:  npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bar-chart.json   To use Britecharts with another framework, use the create, update and destroy methods of the wrappers package. For Angular, check out ngx-britecharts.

searchDocs.title: As a JSON spec​
searchDocs.content: { "$schema": "https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/bar.json", "chart": "bar", "config": { "isHorizontal": true, "a11yTitle": "Signups by plan" }, "data": [{ "name": "Pro", "value": 412 }] }   Editors validate and complete it from the schema, and BarWrapper.create(element, spec.data, spec.config) draws it.

searchDocs.title: Charts​
searchDocs.content: Every chart shares the common accessors (width, height, margin, colorSchema, isLoading, a11yTitle and so on) and adds its own:  API, Demo Line ChartAPI, Demo Bar ChartAPI, Demo Donut ChartAPI, Demo Stacked Bar ChartAPI, Demo Grouped Bar ChartAPI, Demo Stacked Area ChartAPI, Demo Scatter PlotAPI, Demo HeatmapAPI, Demo TreemapAPI, Demo Sparkline ChartAPI, Demo Bullet ChartAPI, Demo Brush ChartAPI, Demo Tooltip, and its single-value presetAPI, Demo Legend  Britecharts is built with the reusable chart pattern on plain D3.js code you can read, fork and modify, and every chart is covered by unit tests and by browser tests in real consumer apps. To customise the look, see Styling Britecharts.

searchDocs.content: Britecharts	Chart.jsDraws on	svg	canvas Screen readers	a name and the data as a table, by default	the canvas is not accessible; you add aria-label, role or fallback content Keyboard through the data	on by default, 8 charts	no Styling	CSS, with --bc-* custom properties	the chart's options; canvas ignores CSS Dark mode	follows the page's color-scheme	set colours in the options Export	PNG and svg, exportChart('chart.svg')	PNG or JPEG data URL, toBase64Image() Chart types	bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, stacked area, donut and pie, heatmap, treemap, scatter plot, bullet, sparkline, brush	bar, line and area, pie and doughnut, scatter, bubble, radar, polar area, mixed, plus community chart types Frameworks	plain JavaScript, React	plain JavaScript; React, Vue, Svelte and Angular through community wrappers License	Apache 2.0	MIT

searchDocs.title: Choose Chart.js when​
searchDocs.content: You draw thousands of points. A canvas draws large datasets faster than an svg with one element per point.You need radar, polar area or bubble charts. Britecharts has none of these.You want its ecosystem. Chart.js is one of the most used chart libraries, with many plugins and answers to most questions online.

searchDocs.title: Choose Britecharts when​
searchDocs.content: Your charts must be accessible. A canvas is one image to a screen reader, and Chart.js leaves its text alternative to you. Britecharts names every chart and renders its data as a table that screen readers can read. It also lets keyboards move through the data. See accessible JavaScript charts.You style with CSS. Every colour around the data is a CSS custom property, and the charts switch to dark mode with your page.You need vector output. exportChart saves an svg with its styles inlined. The svg stays sharp in a document or a design tool.You use React. Britecharts ships its own React components, and a shadcn registry.

searchDocs.title: Move a bar chart​
searchDocs.content: A Chart.js bar chart takes labels and datasets:  new Chart(document.getElementById('uses'), { type: 'bar', data: { labels: ['Shiny', 'Blazing', 'Radiant'], datasets: [{ label: 'Uses', data: [12, 31, 24] }], }, });   A Britecharts bar chart takes one object per bar and draws into any element:  import { bar, tooltip } from '@britecharts/core'; import '@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css'; const data = [ { name: 'Shiny', value: 12 }, { name: 'Blazing', value: 31 }, { name: 'Radiant', value: 24 }, ]; bar() .width(600) .height(300) .a11yTitle('Uses of each word') .tooltip(tooltip()) .render('#uses', data);   Chart.js shows a tooltip by default. In Britecharts, the chart's tooltip setting adds one, as above: see how to add a tooltip. To try both on a page with no build step, use the CDN bundle, or open an example in your browser.  Sources: Chart.js accessibility, Chart.js introduction, Chart.js API, Chart.js integration.

searchDocs.title: Choose Highcharts when​
searchDocs.content: You need its range: stock charts, maps, Gantt charts, or chart types Britecharts doesn't have.You need the deepest accessibility. Highcharts adds sonification, voice input and tactile export.You want commercial support, and the license fits your budget.

searchDocs.title: Choose Britecharts when​
searchDocs.content: You can't buy seats, or don't want to. Britecharts is free for any use under Apache 2.0, including commercial products.You want accessibility without setup. The data table and keyboard navigation are on in every chart, with no module to load. See accessible JavaScript charts.Your charts fit its set: bars, lines, areas, donuts, heatmaps and scatter plots cover most dashboards.You want to own the code. Britecharts is open source, so you can read, patch or fork any chart.

searchDocs.title: Move a column chart​
searchDocs.content: A Highcharts column chart takes categories and series:  Highcharts.chart('uses', { chart: { type: 'column' }, title: { text: 'Uses of each word' }, xAxis: { categories: ['Shiny', 'Blazing', 'Radiant'] }, series: [{ name: 'Uses', data: [12, 31, 24] }], });   A Britecharts bar chart takes one object per bar. Put the title in your page's markup. Give screen readers the same words:  import { bar, tooltip } from '@britecharts/core'; import '@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css'; const data = [ { name: 'Shiny', value: 12 }, { name: 'Blazing', value: 31 }, { name: 'Radiant', value: 24 }, ]; bar() .width(600) .height(300) .a11yTitle('Uses of each word') .tooltip(tooltip()) .render('#uses', data);   Several series, like Highcharts' multi-series column chart, map to the grouped bar chart.  To try Britecharts with nothing to install, open an example in your browser.  Sources: Highcharts accessibility module, Highcharts export module, Highcharts shop, Highcharts integrations.

searchDocs.title: How to Create a Pull Request​
searchDocs.content: When you have a branch that you want to contribute back to Britecharts, you need to create a Pull Request(PR) to propose the addition of the code. Follow these steps:  When you're finished coding, git checkout mainRun git pull upstream main (note that your local main should always reflect upstream main)Run git checkout <your branch>Execute git rebase main & reconcile all conflictsMake sure everything looks OK codewise by running pnpm run checkPush the branch to your fork with git push origin <your branch>Create a new PR, filling the PR template, and adding a link to the original issue filed (if you see "unable to merge", please pull from your upstream and rebase again)Be patient while you wait for the maintainers to check it :)  If you are new to Open Source, you can learn how to create Pull Requests here.

searchDocs.title: How to Modify a Chart in @britecharts/core​
searchDocs.content: This how-to guide helps you in modifying a chart. We assume you already created an issue and got the green light form the maintainers of the project (or maybe you are working your fork if you are not contributing back to Britecharts).  We have created our charts with a Test-First approach, and we encourage you to keep it the same. However, you can also write tests later too. For a TDD workflow, the process of modifying a component would look like this:  Create a new branch for your modificationOn a new terminal, run pnpm run demos in the root folder and navigate to the chart's demo in storybookFind the test of the chart you want to modify in /packages/core/src/charts/<chartName> with at .spec.js extensionWrite a failing test for the API accessor or the feature you want to addOn a new terminal, run pnpm run test from the root folderCheck that the test failsWrite the code that would make that test pass on the chart located in /packages/core/src/charts/<chartName>. Please follow our API Guidelines.Make the test pass by writing the less amount of codeRefactor until you get a nice and clean codeAdd/update the JSDoc comments so that the proper documentation gets generated when you run pnpm run docsCheck the storybook demo to see the code in action (you can also add a new demo there if necessary)Create a pull request and ask the maintainers to review itOnce you have their OK, they will merge your pull request

searchDocs.title: How to Create a New Chart in @britecharts/core​
searchDocs.content: Adding a new chart is a bunch of work, but we hope that using the current code and documentation helps you in the process. The steps are:  Create a new branch for your componentOn a new terminal, run pnpm run demos to see the storybook running.Given that your new chart is chart-name, create a folder within /packages/core/src/charts named chart-name and in the same folder a new test file chart-name.spec.js.Create a new data builder file. Name it something like chartNameChartDataBuilder.js.In the chart folder, create a new chart file called chart-name.js.Create a <chartName>.stories.js file to hold a new demo for the new chart. Re-run the demos script to get it showing in the storybook.Export the new chart from packages/core/src/index.ts, with a camel case name, so it ships in the bundles.Go to your test file /packages/core/src/charts/chart-name.spec.js and, taking another test as an example, copy over pieces until you have the first test case.Add one test and make it fail by calling pnpm run test or keep the tests running with pnpm run test:watch.Keep on coding according to our API GuidelinesOnce you think you are close to having something working, start adding JSDoc comments to your codeGenerate your docs with pnpm run docs and manually test the API definition in the docs site.Create a pull request with your branch and ping one of the core maintainers to get it reviewedOnce you have addressed all the comments and got the green light, the maintainers will merge the PR

searchDocs.content: Britecharts	RechartsFrameworks	React, and plain JavaScript in any page	React API	one component per chart, configured with props	charts composed from JSX parts: axes, grid, bars, tooltip Screen readers	a name and the data as a table, by default	ARIA labels and roles, by default since 3.0; no data table Keyboard through the data	on by default, 8 charts	arrow keys, on by default since 3.0 Export	PNG and svg, with the exportChart prop	none built in Chart types	bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, stacked area, donut and pie, heatmap, treemap, scatter plot, bullet, sparkline, brush	area, bar, line, composed, scatter, pie, radar, radial bar, funnel, treemap, sankey, sunburst shadcn	a registry of chart components	shadcn/ui's chart component License	Apache 2.0	MIT

searchDocs.title: Choose Recharts when​
searchDocs.content: You want to compose a chart from parts, such as a bar and a line on the same axes, or reference lines and areas.You need a funnel, treemap, sankey or radar chart.You already use shadcn/ui's chart component, and want the examples and answers its users share.

searchDocs.title: Choose Britecharts when​
searchDocs.content: Screen readers must read the data. Recharts adds labels and keyboard access. Britecharts also renders each chart's data as a table that screen readers read row by row. See accessible JavaScript charts.Your charts live outside React too. The same charts work in a server-rendered page, a Web Component or a script tag, with one API across both.You want export. exportChart="uses.svg" downloads the chart, with its styles inlined.You want finished charts with fewer decisions. Each chart includes tooltips, loading states and animation, and every chart uses the same prop names.

searchDocs.title: Move a bar chart​
searchDocs.content: A Recharts bar chart composes its parts:  import { BarChart, Bar, XAxis, YAxis, Tooltip } from 'recharts'; <BarChart width={600} height={300} data={data}> <XAxis dataKey="name" /> <YAxis /> <Tooltip /> <Bar dataKey="value" /> </BarChart>;   A Britecharts bar chart reads name and value from each row, and draws its axes itself. The tooltip wraps the chart:  import { Bar, Tooltip } from '@britecharts/react'; import '@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css'; <Tooltip data={data} title="Uses" render={(props) => ( <Bar {...props} width={600} height={300} a11yTitle="Uses of each word" /> )} />;   To fill the container's width, wrap it in ResponsiveContainer, as the React example does. You can also open the example in your browser.  Sources: Recharts README, Recharts 3.0 migration guide, Recharts and accessibility, shadcn/ui chart.

searchDocs.title: Local Development​
searchDocs.content: To start developing this documentation site, run:  $ pnpm start   This command does several things:  Copies over the Readme from the root packageGenerates the API from the @britecharts/core chart commentsStarts a local development server and opens up a browser window  Changes in the markdown files of this package and configuration are reflected live without having to restart the server. However, to update the docs with the latest comments from the packages or the readme, you will need to re-run pnpm start.

searchDocs.title: Build​
searchDocs.content: $ pnpm build   This command generates static content into the build directory and can be served using any static contents hosting service.

searchDocs.title: Checking links​
searchDocs.content: $ pnpm docs:build $ pnpm docs:links   A broken internal link already fails pnpm build, since Docusaurus is set to throw on one. docs:links serves the built site and follows every link on every page, the external ones included, and fails on any that is broken. The Link check workflow runs it on every pull request, on main, and once a week, because links rot with nothing changing on our side. The few hosts it skips, and why, are listed at the top of scripts/check-links.mjs.

searchDocs.title: Deployment*​
searchDocs.content: Using SSH:  $ USE_SSH=true pnpm deploy   Not using SSH:  $ GIT_USER=<Your GitHub username> pnpm deploy   If you are using GitHub pages for hosting, this command is a convenient way to build the website and push to the gh-pages branch.

searchDocs.title: Usage​
searchDocs.content: Every chart in @britecharts/react is a function component: you pass in some props, and it renders a chart.  import { Bar } from '@britecharts/react'; const data = [ { name: 'Vibrant', value: 2, }, { name: 'Opalescent', value: 4, }, { name: 'Shining', value: 3, }, ]; <Bar data={data} width={400} isHorizontal />   Check our Storybook for more examples and check the source to copy/paste code.

searchDocs.title: Loading data​
searchDocs.content: data is required. Pass null while it loads: nothing is drawn until it arrives, and the chart is drawn as soon as it does. Leaving data out, or passing undefined, is an error (and a type error, too).  <Bar data={isLoading ? null : data} />

searchDocs.title: Updating a chart​
searchDocs.content: A chart is redrawn when its props change, and only then. On every render the data and each configuration value are compared with what was last drawn, so a re-render with the same props costs nothing. The consequence is that the data has to be a new array or object to be redrawn: mutating it in place and re-rendering with the same reference does nothing.  setData([...data, newPoint]); // redraws data.push(newPoint); setData(data); // does not: same array, nothing changed

searchDocs.title: No instance, no ref​
searchDocs.content: Function components have no instance to point a ref at, so a ref on a chart is not accepted (the typings say so). A chart is drawn into a <div> the component owns, and removes what it drew when it unmounts.

searchDocs.title: Tooltips​
searchDocs.content: A Tooltip wraps the chart it decorates: give it a render prop that returns the chart, and pass on the props it hands you, which are what connect the two.  The charts name the fields of their data points differently, so some of them need the tooltip told where to look:  Chart	Tooltip propsLine	topicLabel="topics" StackedArea	none StackedBar	nameLabel="stack" GroupedBar	nameLabel="group" ScatterPlot	valueLabel="y" Bar, Donut, Heatmap, Treemap	none  Without them, the tooltip shows no rows (line), rows without their colours (stacked and grouped bar) or no value (scatter plot).  import { Line, Tooltip } from '@britecharts/react'; <Tooltip data={data} render={(props) => <Line {...props} />} topicLabel="topics" title="A title" />

searchDocs.title: Responsive charts​
searchDocs.content: ResponsiveContainer hands its render prop the width it has measured, and measures again when the window is resized. withResponsiveness does the same for a component you wrap, as its width prop (a width you pass yourself wins).  import { Line, ResponsiveContainer, withResponsiveness } from '@britecharts/react'; <ResponsiveContainer render={({ width }) => <Line data={data} width={width} />} /> const ResponsiveLine = withResponsiveness(Line); <ResponsiveLine data={data} />

searchDocs.title: API​
searchDocs.content: Each component's API is a reflection of Britecharts charts and their APIs. They also have a bunch of React specific props, and there are some changes due to the declarative way of building with React.  For example, if we need to check the options of a bar chart, you will first check the bar chart's API in the main project API reference page.  Every Britecharts chart has a component:  Bar charts (API)Brush charts (API)Bullet charts (API)Grouped Bar charts (API)Donut charts (API)Heatmaps (API)Treemaps (API)Line charts (API)Scatter Plots (API)Sparkline charts (API)Stacked Area charts (API)Stacked Bar charts (API)Tooltips (API), wrapping the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts with a list of values, and the bar, scatter plot and heatmap charts with a single value (the mini tooltip)Legends (API)The ResponsiveContainer component and the withResponsiveness function, described above  These components were previously hosted in the britecharts-react repository, but became a package with Britecharts V3.

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: To install run:  pnpm add @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers @britecharts/react   Or, with npm:  npm i --save @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers @britecharts/react   Britecharts-React is available as an NPM module or through CDN links (in different formats or a bundle).  Import the components from the package: bundlers get ES modules, and require('@britecharts/react') gets the UMD bundle. The React consumer in the integration package shows every way of loading it, and is what CI runs.

searchDocs.title: Supported React versions​
searchDocs.content: peerDependencies requires react and react-dom >=16.8: the components use hooks, which arrived in that release. What is actually verified on every commit:  React 19, by the unit tests, which now run on React Testing Library, and in a real browser: CI packs the package the way a release does, installs it into a React 19 project, and loads it in production and in a development build under StrictMode, which runs every effect's setup, cleanup and setup again.  React 17 and 18 are expected to work and are not exercised. If you hit a version-specific problem on an older React, please open an issue.

searchDocs.title: Acknowledgments​
searchDocs.content: For this project, we have followed the approach called ‘Mapping Lifecycle methods’ based on Nicholas Hery's article: a chart's create, update and destroy are called from the component's mount, update and unmount, which one internal hook now does for every chart. We want to recognize all the contributors in the parent project Britecharts.

searchDocs.content: Documentation HomepageContributing GuideCode of Conduct

searchDocs.title: Contribute​
searchDocs.content: When Britecharts adds a chart, check out our how-to guide for creating new charts to bring it to React. Check also the contributing guide if you want to help.  Note that the aim of this project is to allow the usage of Britecharts within your React applications. For that, we are ‘wrapping’ Britecharts with @britecharts/wrappers. This means that any new features need to first be implemented on Britecharts. Only then you could update the props and logic that passes in the configuration.

searchDocs.title: TypeScript​
searchDocs.content: The package is written in TypeScript, and its type declarations are generated from the components at build time. Each component's props type is exported from the package root (BarChartProps, LineProps and so on), and CI compiles a TypeScript project against the packed package.

searchDocs.title: Usage​
searchDocs.content: @britecharts/wrappers components expose a simple API to allow its use in frontend frameworks. This API contains three methods: create, update, and destroy.  To use them, you will pass a configuration object following the Britecharts core component API and a container:  import { BarWrapper } from '@britecharts/wrappers'; const container = document.querySelector('.container'); const data = [ { name: 'Vibrant', value: 2, }, { name: 'Opalescent', value: 4, }, { name: 'Shining', value: 3, }, ]; const configuration = { width: 400, margin: {left: 10}, }; const barInstance = BarWrapper.create(container, data, configuration); //... BarWrapper.update(container, newData, {}, barInstance);   The wrappers include a lightweight configuration and container validation.  A configuration value of undefined or null means "not set" and the chart keeps its own default. Any other value is applied, including the falsy ones: false, 0 and '' reach the chart, so a setting can be turned back off with { isLoading: false }.  In theory, you shouldn't be using this wrappers by themselves, but you might prefer this API (more OO-like) for your vanilla JavaScript projects.

searchDocs.title: API​
searchDocs.content: The API of the wrappers has only three methods: create, update and destroy. Note that each component wrapper's configuration options is a reflection of Britecharts charts' APIs.

searchDocs.title: Create​
searchDocs.content: Creates a new Britechart chart and returns its instance.  Signature:<Wrapper>.create(HTMLElement, <ChartDataShape>, <ConfigurationObject>) => BritechartChart  Example:  const barInstance = BarWrapper.create(container, data, configuration);

searchDocs.title: Update​
searchDocs.content: Updates a chart with new data or configuration.  Signature:<Wrapper>.update(HTMLElement, <ChartDataShape>, <ConfigurationObject>, BritechartChart) => BritechartChart  Example:  BarWrapper.update(container, newData, {}, barInstance);

searchDocs.title: Destroy​
searchDocs.content: Removes the chart's svg from the container, so the container can be used again (a create after a destroy draws exactly one chart). It only removes that svg: never the container itself, which a framework may own, nor anything else inside it.  Signature:<Wrapper>.destroy(HTMLElement) => void  Example:  BarWrapper.destroy(container);   TooltipWrapper.destroy has its own contract: it removes the tooltip from inside the element and never an svg, because a tooltip is created inside the chart it decorates and destroyed against the element around it.

searchDocs.title: Validation​
searchDocs.content: create and update check the configuration before drawing, and throw an error that says what to fix: a key the chart has no accessor for, with the nearest one it does have, and a value of the wrong type, with the type it should be.  Value not supported by Britechart: height chartGradient height: expected a number, got the string "300" chartGradient: expected an array of 2 strings, got an array of 1 Supported accessors: https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/docs/API/bar   An undefined or null value is skipped, and the chart keeps its default.

searchDocs.title: Chart specs and their JSON Schemas​
searchDocs.content: A chart can be written down as a spec: its name, its configuration and its data. Each chart has a JSON Schema for its spec, generated from the TypeScript types the wrappers take, so editors and coding agents can check a spec, and complete it, without running it:  { "$schema": "https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/bar.json", "chart": "bar", "config": { "isHorizontal": true, "a11yTitle": "Signups by plan" }, "data": [{ "name": "Pro", "value": 412 }] }   The schemas are published at https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/<chart>.json and ship in this package as @britecharts/wrappers/schemas/<chart>.json, one per chart, named as core names it (bar, groupedBar, scatterPlot…). Draw a spec with its wrapper: BarWrapper.create(element, spec.data, spec.config). Options that take a function, such as the events and the formatting functions, can't be written in JSON; set them from JavaScript.

searchDocs.title: Availability​
searchDocs.content: Every chart in @britecharts/core has a wrapper: BarWrapper, BrushWrapper, BulletWrapper, DonutWrapper, GroupedBarWrapper, HeatmapWrapper, LegendWrapper, LineWrapper, ScatterPlotWrapper, SparklineWrapper, StackedAreaWrapper, StackedBarWrapper and TreemapWrapper, plus TooltipWrapper for the tooltip.

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: To install run:  pnpm add @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers   Or, with npm:  npm i --save @britecharts/core @britecharts/wrappers

searchDocs.content: Our idea for the short term is to update this package to use TypeScript natively. Let us know if you want to help with it.

searchDocs.content: pnpm demos   starts core on port 2001, React on 2002 and the composed shell on 2000. See the contributing guidefor the details.

searchDocs.title: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
Migration Steps​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: Most of the migration tasks involve changing accessor names, but there are also changes in how we load the modules. Follow these steps to get your application updated in no time:

searchDocs.title: Breaking changes​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: Update the way you load the charts  We moved Britecharts internally from the outdated AMD modules into ES Modules, which changed how you will import the components. See below some examples:  // Version 2 // For ES modules import bar from 'britecharts/dist/umd/bar.min'; // For AMD and CommonJS modules const LineChart = require('britecharts/umd/line.min'); // Version 3 // As ES modules import { bar } from '@britecharts/core'; // As CommonJS modules const { bar } = require('@britecharts/core');   The stylesheets move too. britecharts/dist/css/britecharts.min.css is now @britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css, and each chart's own stylesheet is under @britecharts/core/dist/styles/charts/.  You can also check more ways of loading (CommonJS, UMD and CDN) in the vanilla consumer of our integration tests, which CI runs against every change  Change how you show loading states  Search for any use of the 'loadingState' accessor for getting the loading state, and render the chart with 'isLoading' as true and a valid dataset (it can be empty).  // Version 2 barContainer.html(barChart.loadingState()) // Version 3 barChart .width(containerWidth) .height(300) .isAnimated(true) .isLoading(true) .render(barContainer, dataset);   Use 'valueLocale' to format values  You must use the 'valueLocale' accessor to set the locale object (see the d3-format docs) of the component´s rendered values (axes ticks, numerical values, etc.).  Before, this used to be ´locale´ in the bar, grouped bar, scatted bar, and scatter plot.  // Version 2 barChart .locale({ thousands: '.', grouping: [3], currency: ["$", ""], decimal: "." }) //...other configurations // Version 3 barChart .valueLocale({ thousands: '.', grouping: [3], currency: ["$", ""], decimal: "." }) //...other configurations   In contrast, for time series charts (lineChart, stackedAreaChart), we use 'locale' to pass the language tag for the tooltip to localize the date. It uses Intl.DateTimeFormat, for compatibility and support.  Swap the use 'xAxisCustomFormat' and 'xAxisFormat' on brush charts  Whenever you were using 'xAxisCustomFormat' in a brush chart, now you should use 'xAxisFormat', and viceversa.  // Version 2 brush .xAxisCustomFormat('custom') .xAxisFormat('%A'); // Version 3 brush .xAxisCustomFormat('%A') .xAxisFormat('custom');   This made this configuration consistent with the line and stacked area charts.  Use 'numberFormat' in bar charts  Search for uses of 'valueLabelFormat' and change them to 'numberFormat':  // Version 2 groupedBarChart .valueLabelFormat(',s') // other configurations // Version 3 groupedBarChart .numberFormat(',s') // other configurations   The 'numberFormat' configuration is available for the bar, bullet, donut, grouped bar, stacked-bar, legend, line, mini-tooltip, and tooltip components.  Stop using 'aspectRatio' to set charts' dimensions  We eliminated the 'aspectRatio' accessor from our charts. Instead, use the 'width' and 'height' attributes to set a explicit size and leave the chart to respond to container width changes.  // Version 2 lineChart .width(100) .aspectRatio('0.5'); // Version 3 lineChart .width(100) .height(50)   Expect the typographic minus sign in negative axis labels  Britecharts v3 runs on the current d3 modules, and d3-format changed its default minus sign from the ASCII hyphen (-, U+002D) to the typographic minus (−, U+2212). Negative values on axes and in tooltips now render with the latter.  Nothing to change unless you assert on that text — snapshot tests and string comparisons against axis labels will need updating. If you would rather keep the ASCII hyphen, set it through a value locale on the charts that have one (the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot). The definition needs decimal, thousands, grouping and currency as well:  barChart.valueLocale({ decimal: '.', thousands: ',', grouping: [3], currency: ['$', ''], minus: '-', });   Use the d3 v7 modules alongside Britecharts  Britecharts v3 runs on the d3 v7 generation of the d3-* modules. They are dependencies of @britecharts/core, so installing it from npm installs them, and the ES module and dist/umd builds load them from there rather than bundling them. If your own code uses d3 together with Britecharts, upgrade it to v7 at the same time. The CDN builds under dist/cdn bundle their own copy of d3 and need nothing else on the page.  The two d3 modules Britecharts used that are now deprecated upstream, d3-collection and d3-voronoi, have been replaced internally by d3-array and d3-delaunay. They are no longer dependencies.  Replace the 'dataByTopic' line chart data shape  The line chart no longer accepts the dataByTopic array it required up to 2.10.1. It has taken a flat data array since then, and that is now the only shape it accepts. Passing dataByTopic throws.  // Version 2 lineChart.datum({ dataByTopic: [ { topicName: 'San Francisco', topic: 123, dates: [ { date: '2017-01-16T16:00:00-08:00', value: 1 }, { date: '2017-01-17T16:00:00-08:00', value: 2 } ] } ] }); // Version 3 lineChart.datum({ data: [ { topicName: 'San Francisco', name: 123, date: '2017-01-16T16:00:00-08:00', value: 1 }, { topicName: 'San Francisco', name: 123, date: '2017-01-17T16:00:00-08:00', value: 2 } ] });   One entry per point instead of points nested under each topic, and the topic identifier moves from topic to name. Britecharts groups the data internally, so nothing else about how you configure the chart changes.  If you have data in the old shape, this converts it:  const toFlatData = ({ dataByTopic }) => dataByTopic.flatMap((topic) => topic.dates.map(({ date, value }) => ({ topicName: topic.topicName, name: topic.topic, date, value, })) );   Update custom tooltip handlers on the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts  Every chart now dispatches customMouseMove with the same payload: the hovered data point, its anchor [x, y] in pixels relative to the chart's drawing area, the chart's [width, height], and, from these four charts, the map of topic names to colours. Before, they dispatched (dataPoint, colorMap, x, y). If you wire the tooltip directly, nothing changes; a handler of your own that reads the arguments by position has to take the new order. tooltip.update still accepts the old order in 3.x and warns once.  // Version 2 lineChart.on('customMouseMove', function (dataPoint, colorMap, x, y) { chartTooltip.update(dataPoint, colorMap, x, y); trackHover(dataPoint, x); }); // Version 3 lineChart.on('customMouseMove', function (dataPoint, [x, y], size, colorMap) { chartTooltip.update(dataPoint, [x, y], size, colorMap); trackHover(dataPoint, x); }); // Either version lineChart.on('customMouseMove', chartTooltip.update);   With that, tooltip and miniTooltip are one component: tooltip shows a list or a single value by the shape of the data point (or as told by layout), so use tooltip() everywhere. miniTooltip() still works but is deprecated, logs a warning and goes in version 4. tooltip() also no longer shows the placeholder "Tooltip title": if your tooltips relied on it, set title. The tooltip now keeps itself inside the chart, follows the pointer (the stacked and grouped bar charts show it over a bar only), and its tooltipOffset default is { x: 0, y: 0 } (it was { x: 0, y: -55 }, for a placement that no longer exists). xAxisValueType defaults to 'auto', which shows dates as dates, numbers as numbers and category names as they are; set 'date' or 'number' to force one, as before. In React, Tooltip's customMouseMove callback receives the new order, and Tooltip now wraps the bar, scatter plot and heatmap charts too.  Replace the Step chart  The Step chart is removed from every package: the step export of @britecharts/core, its StepWrapper and the React Step component, with their stylesheets and builds. A bar chart draws the same data.  Transpile for older browsers yourself  The builds now target ES2020 instead of ES5. Every current browser runs them as they are. If you support a browser older than that, transpile Britecharts in your own build, as you would any package that ships modern syntax.  Move from britecharts-react to @britecharts/react  The React components are published as @britecharts/react, and they work differently in a few ways you may rely on:  // Version 2 import { Bar } from 'britecharts-react'; // Version 3 import { Bar } from '@britecharts/react';   React 16.8 or later is required, since the components are now function components built on hooks. They have no instances any more, so a ref on a chart component is not accepted.A chart redraws only when its props change. If you update your data by mutating it in place, pass a new array or object instead.data is required. Pass null while it loads: the chart draws nothing until the data arrives.false, 0 and '' now reach the chart, so isLoading={false} ends a loading state. Leave a prop out, or pass undefined, to keep the chart's default.PropTypes are gone. Each component's props type is exported from the package root (BarChartProps, LineProps and so on) for TypeScript projects.StackedBar's nameLabelFormat prop is removed. No chart had that setting, so passing it threw.axisTimeCombinations is no longer a prop of Line, StackedArea or Tooltip. Import the axisTimeCombinations constant from the package and pass one of its values to xAxisFormat.  Label bullet charts and sparklines outside the chart  The bullet chart no longer draws a title and subtitle, and the sparkline no longer draws a title. Text drawn inside the svg cannot wrap, clips at the chart's edge and does not follow the page's typography, so these charts now draw only the data. The customTitle and customSubtitle accessors and the title and subtitle data fields of the bullet chart are removed, as are the sparkline's titleText and titleTextStyle. The React Bullet and Sparkline components drop the matching props.  Put the label in your own markup next to the chart, and give screen readers the chart's name with a11yTitle:  // Version 2 bulletChart.customTitle('CPU 1').customSubtitle('GHz'); sparklineChart.titleText('Signups'); // Version 3 // <h3>CPU 1 <small>GHz</small></h3> above the chart's container bulletChart.a11yTitle('CPU 1, GHz'); sparklineChart.a11yTitle('Signups');   The legend still draws its own labels.  Load one bundle instead of a file per chart  Version 2 published a UMD file for each chart, like britecharts/dist/umd/bar.min.js. Version 3 publishes one UMD bundle and one CDN bundle with every chart, and ES modules for bundlers. Bundlers keep only the charts you import, so a per-chart file saves nothing there. On a page with a script tag, load the CDN bundle, which includes d3, and use the core global:  <!-- Version 2 --> <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/britecharts/dist/umd/bar.min.js"></script> <script>const barChart = britecharts.bar();</script> <!-- Version 3 --> <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"></script> <script>const barChart = core.bar();</script>   The colors come with the bundle as core.colors. The per-chart stylesheets under dist/styles/charts/ are still published. @britecharts/wrappers and @britecharts/react also publish only their bundles: import the wrappers and components from the package, or use the wrappers and react globals.  The packages are ES modules ("type": "module"), so they load with import in Node as well as in bundlers. require still works and gets the CommonJS bundle, which is now a .cjs file. If you required a bundle by its path, update the extension: @britecharts/core/dist/umd/bundle/core.bundled.min.js is now core.bundled.min.cjs, and likewise for wrappers and react. The CDN bundle keeps its .js name.  Expect null from an accessor you have not set  An accessor that has not been set now reads null on every chart. Before, the same accessor read null on some charts and undefined on others: yAxisLabel on the grouped bar, stacked bar, scatter plot and stacked area, xAxisLabel on the scatter plot, numberFormat on the donut, line and stacked area, and locale on the line, stacked area and tooltip.  A truthiness check works as before. Update code that compares with === undefined, and TypeScript code that annotated the old type: the getters are typed T | null.  // Version 2 if (lineChart.numberFormat() === undefined) { /* ... */ } // Version 3 if (lineChart.numberFormat() === null) { /* ... */ }   Name your data's keys as the charts expect  The accessors that let a chart read its data under other keys are removed: nameLabel and valueLabel on the bar chart, groupLabel, nameLabel and valueLabel on the grouped bar, stackLabel, nameLabel and valueLabel on the stacked bar, dateLabel, topicLabel and valueLabel on the line chart, dateLabel, keyLabel and valueLabel on the stacked area, and dateLabel and valueLabel on the sparkline. They warned that they were deprecated since version 2. The React components drop the matching props.  If you used them, rename the keys in your data to the ones each chart's data shape names, such as name and value for the bar chart:  // Version 2 barChart.nameLabel('letter').valueLabel('frequency'); barContainer.datum([{ letter: 'A', frequency: 0.08 }]).call(barChart); // Version 3 const data = rows.map(({ letter, frequency }) => ({ name: letter, value: frequency })); barChart.render(barContainer, data);   The tooltip keeps its dateLabel, nameLabel, topicLabel and valueLabel: it reads the data points of several charts, and they use different keys.

searchDocs.title: New features​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: Start using TypeScript with Britecharts.  You can now use Britecharts in your TypeScript projects! The packages are written in TypeScript, and their type declarations are generated from that source, so they always match what the charts do. Import the types from the package root: each chart's data shape and module type from @britecharts/core, and each component's props from @britecharts/react.  Stop re-rendering charts when the viewport width changes.  In version 2 and our demos, we recommended listening to viewport width changes and re-render charts with the updated container width. This wasn't necessary, as SVGs provide a viewBox property that allows us to make our charts fully responsive out of the box. That's how Britecharts works starting version 3, so say bye-bye to those window 'resize' listeners!  Use 'colorMap' to select the colors you want for each data category.  One common request of our users was to specify the colors for each category on the different Britecharts components. Now you can! Use the "colorMap" property to specify a hash map between category names and HEX colors.  Specify the duration of animations with 'animationDuration'  Most Britecharts' components have animations that you can activate with the 'isAnimated' configuration. Since version 3, you can also set the duration of those animations in milliseconds with the 'animationDuration' accessor.  Rely on one tooltip for every chart  tooltip renders the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts' lists and the bar, scatter plot, heatmap and donut charts' single values; maxEntries caps the rows, layout forces a layout, xAxisValueType('category') shows a category key as it is. customClick on the stacked and grouped bar charts carries the clicked bar's own data as a third argument.  Chart negative values  The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and brush charts draw negative values, below or to the left of a zero baseline. They used to throw on a negative datum. The scatter plot's value axis now runs below zero when the data does, and each circle's size shows the magnitude of its value. Before, points with a negative value were not drawn.  Show a loading state on every chart  isLoading now covers every data chart, including the bullet, heatmap and scatter plot, each with a skeleton in its own shape.  Name your charts for screen readers  Every chart gives its svg a role and an accessible name, so a screen reader announces it as an image called, for example, "Bar chart". Set a11yTitle to name it after what it shows, and a11yDescription to add a sentence that screen readers read after the name. The React components take both as props.  barChart .a11yTitle('Monthly visits') .a11yDescription('Visits doubled in May');   Draw charts with 'render', and give them a 'tooltip'  render draws a chart into a CSS selector, an element or a d3 selection, so a page needs no d3 code of its own. The tooltip setting connects and places a tooltip, and sets the labels the chart's data points need. Your version 2 code, container.datum(data).call(chart) and the tooltip wired by hand, keeps working.  // Version 2 barChart .on('customMouseOver', chartTooltip.show) .on('customMouseMove', chartTooltip.update) .on('customMouseOut', chartTooltip.hide); barContainer.datum(data).call(barChart); barContainer.select('.metadata-group').datum([]).call(chartTooltip); // Version 3 barChart.tooltip(tooltip()).render(barContainer, data);

searchDocs.title: Summary of Changes​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: We changed many things in the third version of Britecharts; here are some summaries:

searchDocs.title: Breaking Changes​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Migration Guide from version 2 to version 3
searchDocs.content: New monorepo organization of the code with @britecharts/core and @britecharts/react as the main packages.The builds target ES2020 instead of ES5.Runs on the d3 v7 modules; negative numbers render with the typographic minus sign.Removes the Step chart from every package.Removes the line chart's 'dataByTopic' data shape.Publishes one UMD bundle and one CDN bundle instead of a UMD file per chart. The per-chart stylesheets stay.The packages are ES modules: import works in Node, and the CommonJS bundles require loads end in .cjs.Removes the data-key accessors ('nameLabel', 'valueLabel', 'dateLabel', 'topicLabel', 'keyLabel', 'groupLabel', 'stackLabel') from the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, stacked area and sparkline charts, and the matching React props. The tooltip keeps its own.An accessor that has not been set reads null on every chart, never undefined.Removes the bullet chart's title and subtitle ('customTitle', 'customSubtitle' and the 'title' and 'subtitle' data fields) and the sparkline's title ('titleText', 'titleTextStyle'), with the matching React props.Changes 'loadingMarkup' option into an explicit option for 'isLoading' in most of the charts.Adds 'valueLocale' or renames 'locale' into 'valueLocale' for formatting values in the bar chart, grouped bar chart, scatter plot, and stacked bar.Fixes the custom format feature in the line and stacked area chart, renaming 'xAxisFormat' into 'xAxisCustomFormat' and 'xAxisCustomFormat' into 'xAxisFormat'. The time combinations are exported as constants.axisTimeCombinations.Renames value formatting functions into 'numberFormat' in the grouped bar and stacked bar charts.Removed the 'aspectRatio' configuration chart from the line, scatter plot, stacked area, bullet, grouped bar, stacked bar.Changed 'exportChart' to return a promise.The line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts dispatch 'customMouseMove' as (dataPoint, [x, y], [width, height], colorMap), the same payload as every other chart; tooltip.update still accepts the old (dataPoint, colorMap, x, y) order and warns once. React's Tooltip passes the new order to its 'customMouseMove' callback.The tooltip's 'tooltipOffset' defaults to { x: 0, y: 0 } and 'xAxisValueType' to 'auto'.The stacked and grouped bar charts show the tooltip, and dispatch 'customClick', only over a bar.React: the components are function components, need React 16.8 or later, redraw only when their props change, and pass false, 0 and '' on to the chart. PropTypes, StackedBar's nameLabelFormat prop and the axisTimeCombinations prop are removed.
