searchDocs.title: General Considerations​
searchDocs.content: Variable and accessor names should be camel cased (eg. "shouldBeCamelCase"), and we try to use only one word that is the same as the internal variable we are using. Variables are nouns, while commands are verbs.  For example: height, width, margin, title.

searchDocs.title: Variable and function names length​
searchDocs.content: We will follow the 'Scope Rule':  Variable names: short in small scopes (d)long in large scopes (percentageLabelMargin) Functions names: short in large scopes like public commands (hide, width)long in small scopes (drawVerticalExtendedLine)

searchDocs.title: Event dispatchers​
searchDocs.content: The custom events that are attached to the charts always are prefixed with ‘on’.  As in: .on('customHover')

searchDocs.title: Booleans​
searchDocs.content: We want them to be predicates. They are prefixed with one of the following:  shouldhasis  As in: isAnimated, hasFixedHighlightedSlice.

searchDocs.title: Commands​
searchDocs.content: Commands must be verbs and be constructed into a single word if possible  As in: hide, show, exportChart

searchDocs.title: Data labels​
searchDocs.content: For API entries that configure the keys of the input data, we use the property name and the suffix ‘label’.  As in: dateLabel, valueLabel

searchDocs.title: Formats​
searchDocs.content: A simple name with the property name and ‘format’ suffix.  As in: numberFormat, xLabelFormat

searchDocs.title: Ticks and Axis​
searchDocs.content: We use the axis name followed by the 'axis' and ‘ticks’ suffix:  As in: xTicks, yTicks

searchDocs.title: Building the packages​
searchDocs.content: Each published package is built from pnpm build in its folder, or all three at once with pnpm build:packages at the root. Babel writes the ES modules file by file and only strips the TypeScript types, and tsc writes the declarations. Core's UMD bundle, CDN bundle and stylesheets come from vite build with packages/core/vite.config.js, one run per mode. Wrappers' UMD and CommonJS bundles come from one vite build with packages/wrappers/vite.config.js. React's UMD bundle comes from vite build with packages/react/vite.config.js. The Storybooks run on Storybook 10's Vite builders, each with its own .storybook/vite.config.mjs. The output targets ES2020.  What comes out of packages/core/dist:  Path	Contentsumd/bundle/core.bundled.min.cjs	Every chart in one UMD bundle: the package's main, and what require loads. types-cjs/	The type declarations again, marked CommonJS, for the require condition. cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js	The same, built for a <script> tag, with d3 bundled in. styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css	Every stylesheet. styles/charts/common.min.css, styles/charts/<chart>.min.css	The shared styles, and one file per chart to use alongside them.  The wrappers package emits a UMD and a CommonJS bundle; the React package a UMD bundle. pnpm build at the root builds the three packages, this site and the Storybooks.

searchDocs.title: Styles​
searchDocs.content: The stylesheets are SCSS under packages/core/src/styles, written with the Sass module system (@use): britecharts.scss is the whole set, common.scss what every chart needs, and charts/<chart>.scss one chart. They compile through core's Vite build; pnpm lint:styles runs stylelint over them.

searchDocs.title: Tasks​
searchDocs.content: From the root:  Task	Descriptionpnpm test	Runs the Vitest suites of every package; pnpm test:ci is the same command as CI runs it, and pnpm test:watch watches. pnpm test:integration	Packs the three packages with pnpm's packer, installs them into the vanilla, TypeScript and React 19 consumers and checks tarball contents, require() paths, the typings and, in Chromium, that every way of loading a chart renders and every tooltip stays inside its chart. pnpm lint	ESLint over every package (pnpm lint:js) and stylelint over the styles (pnpm lint:styles). pnpm format runs oxfmt. pnpm check	Both linters, the type-check and the test suite, what CI runs. pnpm build / pnpm build:packages	Everything, or only the three published packages. pnpm demos	Serves the core, React and composed Storybooks together on ports 2001, 2002 and 2000. pnpm docs / pnpm docs:build	Serves or builds this site, after copying the READMEs in and generating the API pages from the charts' JSDoc. pnpm docs:links	Serves the built site and follows every link on it, external ones included; the Link check workflow runs it on every pull request and weekly. pnpm changeset	Records what a change does and which packages it bumps, for the release. pnpm version-packages	Applies the pending changesets: bumps versions and writes the changelogs. pnpm release	Builds the packages and publishes every non-private workspace, in dependency order.

searchDocs.title: Docs and Storybooks​
searchDocs.content: The API reference is generated: packages/docs/scripts/generate-docs.js runs jsdoc-to-markdown over packages/core/src and writes one page per chart into docs/API, and copy-readme.js brings the READMEs in. The three Storybooks build with pnpm build:demos and are deployed next to the site, under /storybook/, by scripts/compose-site.js, so composition is same-origin.

searchDocs.title: Releases​
searchDocs.content: Versions are managed with Changesets. @britecharts/core, @britecharts/wrappers and @britecharts/react are a fixed group, so they always share a version; the docs, demos and integration packages are never published. The Release workflow publishes from main once the pending changesets are applied, the Integration check gates every merge, and the Smoke workflow re-checks the published packages from npm and jsDelivr afterwards. MAINTAINING.md has the steps.

searchDocs.title: How to Customize the Chart's Colors​
searchDocs.content: Follow these steps to customize Britecharts' charts to use different color schemas:  Find out if your chart supports the .colorSchema() configuration, if so, keep on readingCheck the Color Palettes demo page and find a palette you likeImport the colors helper at the top of your fileSet the color palette with .colorSchema(colors.colorSchemas.orange) or with any other color schemaDraw the chart  For readers with colour blindness, use colors.colorSchemas.okabeIto. Its eight colours, from Okabe and Ito's palette, stay distinct with the common kinds of colour blindness. Black comes last, so charts with up to seven categories never draw a series in black. Its yellow, orange and sky blue are light on a white background, so the palette suits filled marks such as bars and donut slices better than thin lines. Colour shouldn't be the only thing that tells series apart: a legend or labels help every reader.  Note that in some charts we can only configure a gradient. Use the colorGradients object instead of colorSchemas within the colors helper. You can explore other options in the source code of the colors file.

searchDocs.title: Give each category its own colour​
searchDocs.content: A palette assigns colours in order, so a category's colour changes when the data does. To pin one colour to each category, pass colorMap an object from category to colour:  barChart.colorMap({ Shiny: '#39c2c9', Blazing: '#fcc870', });   A category the map leaves out keeps its palette colour. Each chart matches the keys against one field of its data:  Chart	colorMap keys matchBar, donut, scatter plot, stacked area	name Line	name, the topic's identifier (not topicName) Stacked bar	stack Grouped bar	group  The legend takes colorMap too: pass it the same object so its entries match the chart. In React, colorMap is a prop with the same shape.

searchDocs.title: How to Theme a Chart and Support Dark Mode​
searchDocs.content: Everything around the data (text, axes, grid lines, tooltips, the legend, loading skeletons) takes its colour from a CSS custom property. Each defaults to a light and a dark value, picked by the color-scheme the chart inherits from your page.  To follow the system's light or dark setting, declare both schemes on your page:  :root { color-scheme: light dark; }   To force one, set color-scheme: light or color-scheme: dark on the page, or on any element around the chart. An app with its own light/dark switch sets it there. A page that declares no colour scheme keeps the charts light, as before.  To change a colour, set its token on the charts:  .britechart { --bc-text-muted: #555; --bc-background: #10141a; /* the colour behind your charts */ }   Token	Colours--bc-text	tooltip values and other primary text --bc-text-muted	tick labels, data labels, tooltip titles --bc-text-subtle	axis titles --bc-axis	tick marks, the lines that extend the axes, custom line annotations --bc-grid, --bc-grid-highlight	grid lines, and a highlighted one --bc-background	what is behind the chart: the line chart's drawing mask and an export's background. It defaults to Canvas, the page's background in the current scheme; set it if your page uses another. --bc-surface	the tooltip box, data point markers, hollow circles, heatmap borders --bc-border	the tooltip's border and the hover marker --bc-skeleton, --bc-skeleton-strong	loading states --bc-brush-area, --bc-brush-area-missing	the brush's area, and its gaps --bc-sparkline-area-start, --bc-sparkline-area-end	the sparkline's default area gradient  The data colours come from colorSchema and colorMap, not from these tokens. Exports carry the resolved colours, so an image exported in dark mode keeps its dark background. Browsers without light-dark() (before 2024) show the light values.

searchDocs.title: How to Add a Tooltip to a Chart​
searchDocs.content: Give the chart a tooltip with its tooltip setting. The same tooltip() works on every chart that takes one: the line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts list one row per topic, and the bar, heatmap and scatter plot show one value. It has no title until you set one, and it shows a single value with two decimals unless you set a numberFormat. The donut has no tooltip: it shows the hovered slice in its centre instead.  stackedBar() .tooltip(tooltip().title('Visits')) .render('.js-chart', data);   The chart does the rest, on every draw. It shows the tooltip when the pointer or the keyboard reaches a data point, moves it as they move and hides it when they leave. It draws the tooltip in place, and sets the labels that tell the tooltip which fields of its data points to read, unless you set them on the tooltip yourself. Set tooltip(null) to remove it. A tooltip belongs to one chart, so give each chart its own.

searchDocs.title: Connect a tooltip by hand​
searchDocs.content: To change the data point before the tooltip shows it, connect the tooltip yourself.  Drawing the tooltip by hand takes d3's select, which the tooltip setting does not need. With npm, run npm install d3-selection and import select from it. On a CDN page, add <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/d3-selection@3.0.0/dist/d3-selection.min.js"></script> and call d3.select.  Connect the chart's customMouseOver, customMouseMove and customMouseOut events to the tooltip's show, update and hideTell the tooltip where the chart keeps its data, if the table below lists a setting for itDraw the chart, then call the tooltip on the chart's .metadata-group (for the line and stacked area, on .metadata-group .vertical-marker-container)  import { stackedBar, tooltip } from '@britecharts/core'; import { select } from 'd3-selection'; const stackedBarChart = stackedBar(); const chartTooltip = tooltip() .topicLabel('values') .nameLabel('stack'); stackedBarChart .on('customMouseOver', chartTooltip.show) .on('customMouseMove', chartTooltip.update) .on('customMouseOut', chartTooltip.hide) .render('.js-chart', data); select('.js-chart .metadata-group').datum([]).call(chartTooltip);   The charts do not all name the fields of the data point they send the tooltip the same way, so some need a setting. The tooltip setting sets these for you. By hand, or with React's Tooltip, set them yourself; without them, the tooltip shows no rows, rows without their colours, or no value:  Chart	Tooltip settings	React Tooltip propsLine	none	topicLabel="topics" Stacked area	topicLabel('values')	none Stacked bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('stack')	nameLabel="stack" Grouped bar	topicLabel('values'), nameLabel('group')	nameLabel="group" Scatter plot	valueLabel('y')	valueLabel="y" Bar, heatmap	none	none  React's Tooltip starts from topicLabel('values'), which is why the line chart is the one that needs a prop there. The tooltip reference describes each setting, and the Storybook shows each chart with its tooltip configured.

searchDocs.title: How to Format Numbers and Dates for Your Language​
searchDocs.content: Three settings control how values read. They do different things, so check which one a chart has in its API reference:  numberFormat takes a d3-format specifier, such as ',.2f' for two decimals with a thousands separator, or '.0%' for a percentage. It formats the values on the chart's axes and labels; the tooltip has a numberFormat of its own.valueLocale takes a d3-format locale definition and sets the separators and currency those values use. The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot charts have it. The definition needs at least decimal, thousands, grouping and currency, or the chart throws.locale takes a language tag such as 'fr-FR', and localizes the dates in the tooltip and the brush with Intl.DateTimeFormat.  barChart .numberFormat(',.2f') .valueLocale({ decimal: ',', thousands: '.', grouping: [3], currency: ['', ' €'], }); // The axis reads 1.000,00 instead of 1,000.00   Negative numbers use the typographic minus sign (−), as d3-format does. To get the ASCII hyphen back, add minus: '-' to the locale definition.  Each chart keeps its valueLocale to itself, so two charts on a page can use different ones.

searchDocs.title: How to Show a Loading State​
searchDocs.content: Every data chart can draw a skeleton in its own shape while the data loads:  Set isLoading(true) and draw the chart with whatever data you have, even an empty arrayWhen the data arrives, set isLoading(false) and draw the chart again with it  barChart.isLoading(true).render('.js-chart', []); fetchData().then((data) => { barChart.isLoading(false).render('.js-chart', data); });   In React, pass isLoading together with the data you have, an empty array included, and set it to false when the data arrives. With data={null}, the component draws nothing at all, skeleton included.

searchDocs.title: How to Animate a Chart​
searchDocs.content: Charts draw without animation by default. Set isAnimated(true) to animate them as they draw, and animationDuration to set how long that takes, in milliseconds (1200 by default):  lineChart.isAnimated(true).animationDuration(600);   animationDuration does nothing while isAnimated is false. The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, line, stacked area, donut, heatmap, treemap, scatter plot, sparkline and brush charts animate. React components take both as props.  A reader whose system asks for reduced motion (the prefers-reduced-motion setting) sees every chart drawn without animation, whatever isAnimated is set to. Charts check it each time they draw, so changing the setting applies from the next render. isAnimated() still reads back the value you set. The rest of the motion stops too: tooltips appear and move without fading or easing, the legend drops entries without a fade, and a hovered point is highlighted without its bounce.

searchDocs.title: How to Export a Chart​
searchDocs.content: Call exportChart with a filename to download the chart as it is drawn. The filename picks the format: one ending in .svg downloads an svg file, and any other a png. An optional second argument adds a title at the top:  barChart.exportChart('visits.svg', 'Visits by month'); barChart.exportChart('visits.png');   The svg keeps the chart's styles inlined, so it looks the same in a design tool or a document, and it stays sharp at any size. exportChart returns a promise that resolves once the download starts. In React, every chart component except Brush and Legend takes the filename as its exportChart prop. Setting it downloads the chart once, so set a new filename to download again.

searchDocs.title: How to Chart Negative Values​
searchDocs.content: The bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts draw negative values with no setting to turn on:  The bar charts draw bars below, or to the left of, a zero baseline, and a stacked bar stacks its negative parts down from zero.The scatter plot's value axis runs below zero when the data does, and a circle's size shows the size of its value, so -50 draws as large as 50.  The line and stacked area charts plot negative values as they are. Axis labels for negative numbers use the typographic minus sign: see how to format numbers to change it.

searchDocs.title: How to Make a Chart Accessible​
searchDocs.content: For an overview with live charts to try, and how other libraries compare, see Accessible JavaScript Charts.  Every chart gives its svg a role and a name that screen readers announce: "Bar chart" by default. Name it after what it shows, and add a sentence about what it means:  barChart .a11yTitle('Monthly visits') .a11yDescription('Visits doubled in May');   The name goes in an aria-label, so browsers do not show it as a tooltip on hover. React components take a11yTitle and a11yDescription as props.

searchDocs.title: Read the data as a table​
searchDocs.content: Every chart but the legend also renders its data as a table, right after its svg, which screen readers reach as a table: they can read it row by row, move along a row or down a column, and hear each cell's headings. It is hidden from sight, takes no room on the page, and is linked from the chart with aria-details. Its caption is the chart's name, so set a11yTitle and the table is named after it too.  Charts with several series lay it out wide, as a reader would expect: a line chart has a row per date and a column per topic, and a heatmap a row per day and a column per hour.  The table is on by default. If your page already shows the data in an accessible form, turn it off:  barChart.a11yDataTable(false);   In React, pass a11yDataTable={false}; in the wrappers, a11yDataTable: false in the configuration.

searchDocs.title: Move through the data with a keyboard​
searchDocs.content: The bar, donut, grouped bar, heatmap, line, scatter plot, stacked area and stacked bar charts can be explored without a pointer. Each chart is one stop in the page's tab order; once it has focus:  Key	DoesRight or Left arrow	moves to the next or previous data point: a bar, a slice, a date, a point Down or Up arrow	the same, except on the heatmap, where they move a day Home, End	moves to the first or last point Escape	lets go of the point; leaving the chart does too  The chart responds as it does to a pointer: the point is highlighted, the tooltip follows focus, and the customMouseOver, customMouseMove and customMouseOut events fire, so your own hover code works from the keyboard too. The browser's focus ring shows which chart has focus.  It is on by default. To take the charts out of the tab order, for example in a list of thumbnails, turn it off:  barChart.a11yKeyboardNavigation(false);   In React, pass a11yKeyboardNavigation={false}; in the wrappers, a11yKeyboardNavigation: false in the configuration.

searchDocs.title: Label a bullet chart or a sparkline​
searchDocs.content: The bullet chart and the sparkline draw only their data, with no title: text inside an svg cannot wrap and ignores the page's typography. Put the label in your own markup, next to the chart, and give screen readers the same words:  <h3>CPU load <small>GHz</small></h3> <div class="js-bullet-chart"></div>   bulletChart.a11yTitle('CPU load, GHz').render('.js-bullet-chart', data);

searchDocs.title: How to Describe a Chart as a Spec and Check It​
searchDocs.content: A chart can be written down as a spec, a plain object with its name, its configuration and its data, which you can store, send from a server, or have a coding agent write:  { "$schema": "https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/bar.json", "chart": "bar", "config": { "isHorizontal": true, "a11yTitle": "Signups by plan" }, "data": [{ "name": "Pro", "value": 412 }] }   Each chart has a JSON Schema for its spec at https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/<chart>.json: bar, brush, bullet, donut, groupedBar, heatmap, legend, line, scatterPlot, sparkline, stackedArea, stackedBar, tooltip and treemap. They are generated from the charts' TypeScript types, so they list every accessor with its type and description. With the $schema line, editors such as VS Code check and complete the spec as you type, and any JSON Schema validator (Ajv, for example) can check one before you draw it.  Draw a spec with the chart's wrapper, which checks it too:  import { BarWrapper } from '@britecharts/wrappers'; BarWrapper.create(element, spec.data, spec.config);   A key the chart doesn't have, or a value of the wrong type, throws an error that names each one and says what it should be. Options that take a function, such as the events and the formatting functions, can't be written in JSON: set them from JavaScript.

searchDocs.title: How to Add a Chart to a shadcn App​
searchDocs.content: Britecharts has a shadcn registry, so in an app set up with shadcn/ui one command adds a chart:  npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bar-chart.json   It copies a component into components/charts/bar-chart.tsx, installs @britecharts/react and @britecharts/core, and adds a rule to your CSS that colours the charts with your shadcn theme: text with --foreground and --muted-foreground, axes and grid with --border, tooltips with --popover. The charts follow your app's light and dark modes, and the data keeps Britecharts' palettes. The component is yours to edit.  import { BarChart } from '@/components/charts/bar-chart'; <BarChart data={data} height={300} tooltipTitle="Signups" a11yTitle="Signups by plan" />;   Each chart fills the width of its container, so put it in an element that has a width, and comes with its tooltip set up. Every other prop is the chart's own, as on its API page.  Chart	Add it withBar	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bar-chart.json Grouped bar	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/grouped-bar-chart.json Line	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/line-chart.json Scatter plot	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/scatter-plot.json Stacked area	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/stacked-area-chart.json Stacked bar	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/stacked-bar-chart.json Heatmap	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/heatmap.json Treemap	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/treemap.json Donut	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/donut-chart.json Sparkline	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/sparkline.json Brush	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/brush.json Bullet	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/bullet-chart.json Legend	npx shadcn@latest add https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/legend.json  The registry's index, for shadcn list and shadcn's MCP server, is at https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/r/registry.json.

searchDocs.title: How to Configure Time Scales​
searchDocs.content: Britecharts has some logic to try guessing the best date format on time series charts from the time period of the dataset. As we haven't bulletproofed this algorithm, and sometimes users want specific formats, we also expose configuration options to set custom formats.  The next steps apply to time series charts like the line chart, stacked area chart and brush chart:  Render the chart using the default settings, see if the x-axis format is satisfactory. If not, keep on reading.Check the chart's reference to find out the configuration options, for example, the line chart referenceCheck the options within the axisTimeCombinations object of the chart instance:  console.log('combinations', line.axisTimeCombinations); // Returns { MINUTE_HOUR: 'minute-hour', HOUR_DAY: 'hour-daymonth', DAY_MONTH: 'day-month', MONTH_YEAR: 'month-year', CUSTOM: 'custom' }   Set the xAxisFormat parameter to a value from the ones below (except 'custom')Draw the chart and see if it meets your criteria. If not, try with other time combination. If still doesn't feel right, see next step.Set the xAxisFormat parameter to the value 'custom'Set the xAxisCustomFormat parameter to a valid D3.js time format specifier string. For example: line.xAxisCustomFormat('%H')Play around with different specifiers until finding something that works. You can experiment in this block example.  Remember that for increased accuracy, all date formats in Britecharts should be provided in ISO 8601 Extended Format.

searchDocs.title: Test Driven Development​
searchDocs.content: D3.js charts are complex systems. As other Software Development projects, they start simple and become bloated at the end of the process. To overcome this, we have followed a component approach that allows us to create easily testable units.  We use Vitest as our test runner, with jsdom standing in for the browser.  To start running our tests you would need to follow these steps:  Fork the repository by clicking the fork button on GithubClone the repository with:git clone https://github.com/<your handle>/britecharts.gitGet into the repository folder and install the dependencies with:pnpm installRun the tests with:pnpm run test  This process watches the test and chart files, re-running the tests when those change.

searchDocs.title: JSDoc Generated Documentation​
searchDocs.content: JSDoc is an API documentation generator. It allows us to follow a methodology when commenting our code so that later we can automatically generate documentation from these comments. Check its getting started guide to know more about it.  We enforce jsDoc comments in our review process, hence each function should be commented. We require also to be mindful and when we change the code of a function. Please check if comments need to be updated too. This is essential, as our documentation gets generated from these JSDoc comments.

searchDocs.title: Project Structure​
searchDocs.content: Britecharts is a pnpm workspace with six packages under packages/:  Package	Descriptioncore	The charts, the tooltip and legend, their styles and their TypeScript typings. What @britecharts/core publishes. wrappers	create/update/destroy wrappers around each chart, the seam for framework integrations. Published as @britecharts/wrappers. react	React components built on the wrappers. Published as @britecharts/react. docs	This site: Docusaurus, with the API reference generated from the charts' JSDoc and the READMEs copied in. demos	The Storybook shell that composes the core and React Storybooks into one. integration	Packs the three published packages and installs them into vanilla, TypeScript and React consumer projects to test what ships. Runs on every pull request.  Inside packages/core/src:  Path	Contentsindex.ts	The public entry: the 14 charts, tooltip, miniTooltip, legend, brush, colors and constants. This list is frozen for 3.x and held by the integration tests. charts/<chart>/	One folder per chart: <chart>.ts, which also declares the chart's types, its <chart>.spec.js, its <chart>.stories.js for Storybook, a <chart>DataBuilder.js and the JSON fixtures the specs and stories share. The tooltip folder also holds the modules it is built from (frame.ts, place.ts, motion.ts). charts/helpers/	Code shared by the charts, listed below. styles/	The SCSS: britecharts.scss (everything), common.scss (what every chart needs), charts/<chart>.scss, and the palette and loading-state partials under helpers/. typings/	Types shared across charts under common/, and the types of the colors and constants helpers under helpers/. The published declarations are generated from the sources at build time, and the integration package compiles a TypeScript consumer against them.

searchDocs.title: Code Structure​
searchDocs.content: We require contributors to preserve both the structure and the code standards based on the original Reusable Chart API. The structure of a @britecharts/core chart would look more or less like this:   // D3 module imports // helper imports // Constants // Module definition JSDoc comment // Data definition JSDoc comment export default function module() { // Private variables (more or less grouped) // Extractor functions // Format functions function exports (_selection) { // Locale formatter setup (if any) _selection.each(function (_data) { // Dimension setting // Data cleaning with 'cleanData' function buildSVG(this); // Main building blocks (optional) buildScales(); buildAxis(); drawGridLines(); drawAxis(); drawElements(); // Conditional building blocks } } // Building block definitions // API definitions ordered alphabetically }   We like to do some light 'data cleaning' inside the cleanData method. That would usually include making sure that numbers are not strings. We also use a reduce function, so we create a copy of the original data and cast only the usual quantities or values we need for creating the chart.  Note that most of the building blocks depend on the chart type. For example, on the donut chart, we won't need to create axis or draw them so that those blocks won't be there.  Every chart dispatches the same hover events, customMouseOver, customMouseMove and customMouseOut, with the same payload, so the tooltip is wired the same way to all of them; the tooltip's API page has the table.

searchDocs.title: Core Helpers​
searchDocs.content: Within the core package, we have a set of helpers:  axis Exposes getTimeSeriesAxis, the method that allows conditional formatting depending on the time series values.  classes Turns a list of class names into the class attribute value or the matching CSS selector.  color The color helper contains the objects with the color schemas, the color gradients, and their human-friendly names. Exported as colors.  constants Reusable constants used throughout the project, such as the axis time combinations. Exported as constants.  date Date related methods like addDays, diffDays, getLocaleDateFormatter and similar.  domain getValueDomain builds a value domain that always contains zero, and getBaselineExtent says where a mark growing from that baseline starts and how long it is, so negative values render on the other side of the axis. The bar charts and the brush use them; see the Domain helpers page.  export This helper provides methods that enable the chart export feature of Britecharts.  filter Includes methods for creating SVG effects based on SVG filters. Provides blur and glows.  grid Exposes helpers to create horizontal, vertical or full grids, with the axis baseline and the zero-line highlight. Used in most charts; see the Grid helpers page.  load The load helper provides SVG components that render the loading state of each chart.  locale Keeps code helpers like localeFormatterFor and isValidLocaleDefinion for helping with localization features.  number The number file supports developers by supplying methods that relate to numbers and number formatting. Includes a unique id generator, an integer checker and a method to calculate percentages.  project The deprecation message the charts print when a deprecated data-key accessor is used.  style Methods for serializing styles used in the export feature.  text Functions to help with text related operations like wrapping text on a given width, adding ellipsis when not enough space is available or measuring text length.  type Small type checks and casts, such as isDefined.

searchDocs.title: Labels​
searchDocs.content: On Britecharts, we aim to be methodical on using issue labels, offering our community a way to understand what are the issues about and their status within or development process. We use a bunch of GitHub labels. They are a mix of custom labels and the default Github labels for open-source projects. We base these labels on four main types: status labels, issue type labels, and the “other” category. Read on to learn more about them.  Status Labels​  They show at a glance the status and progress of each issuePrefixed with "status:", followed by the labelOnly one status label will be applied to any particular issue  Labels​  status:needs_triage – For all issues that need to be processed status:needs_reproducing – For bugs that need to be reproduced in order to get fixed status:needs_votes – Issue or bug fix that needs support from the community to be considered status:needs_design – Issue that needs design input to continue. status:in_progress – Issue that is being worked on right now. status:completed – Issue is completed and on main status:abandoned – Issue we won’t go ahead and implement, or that needs a “champion” to take it through status:blocked – Issue blocked by any reason (dependencies, previous work, lack of resources, etc.) The resulting Feature Flow is: Needs Triage >> Needs Votes >> Needs Design >> In Progress >> CompletedOutside the flow: Blocked || Abandoned The resulting Issue Flow is: Needs Triage >> Needs Reproducing >> Needs Votes >> In Progress >> CompletedOutside the flow: Blocked || Abandoned  Here is a diagram representing these states within the lifecycles:  Type Labels​  They show the type of the issuePrefixed with "Type:", followed by the label  Labels​  type:bug – An unexpected problem or unintended behaviortype:feature – A new feature requesttype:maintenance – A regular maintenance chore or task, including refactors, build system, CI, performance improvementstype:documentation – A documentation improvement tasktype:question – An issue or PR that needs more information or a user question  Other Labels​  Some of these are part of the standard GitHub labels and intended for OSS contributorsSome are related to the tools we use to maintain the libraryThey are not prefixed  Labels​  help wanted – Indicates we are looking for contributors on this issue.good first issue – Indicates the issue is a great one to tackle by newcomers to the project or OSS in general.dependencies – For snyk, to manage dependencies updates

searchDocs.title: Install with NPM​
searchDocs.content: The recommended way of installing Britecharts is to use npm or pnpm:  npm install --save @britecharts/core   Or, using pnpm:  pnpm add @britecharts/core   Notice this requires you to have in place a bundling system (Webpack, Parcel, Rollup, or Similar). If you want to drop a script in an HTML file and start working, use the CDN way below.  To use the modules within your JavaScript code, you will follow a different approach depending on the type of modules you are using:  // For CommonJS modules const { bar } = require('@britecharts/core'); // For ES modules import { bar } from '@britecharts/core'; bar().render('.bar-container', data);   The charts draw with render, so you don't need d3 in your own code. searchDocs.title: The Reusable Chart API
searchDocs.content: The Reusable Chart API The Reusable Chart API is a modular structure to create and reuse D3.js components. We saw the first example of this pattern in Mike Bostock’s seminal post Towards Reusable Charts (2012). We built Britecharts using this design pattern, so that all our components benefit from its characteristics. They are all simple, modular, reusable, composable, and testable. The pattern is based in a closure that allows us to keep properties private and define the elements of the components' API. Take a look at the code: /** * This function creates the graph using the selection as container * @param {D3Selection} _selection A d3 selection that represents * the container(s) where the chart(s) will be rendered */ function exports(_selection) { /* @param {object} _data The data to attach and generate the chart */ _selection.each(function (_data) { chartWidth = width - margin.left - margin.right; chartHeight = height - margin.top - margin.bottom; data = _data; buildScales(); buildAxis(); buildSVG(this); buildContainerGroups(); drawBars(); drawAxis(); }); } /** * Gets or Sets the margin of the chart * @param {object} _x Margin object to get/set * @return { margin | module} Current margin or Bar Chart module to chain calls * @public */ exports.margin = function (_x) { if (!arguments.length) { return margin; } margin = _x; return this; }; return exports; This piece of code returns a function that accepts a D3.js selection as input. Then, it extracts the data of that selection to build a chart, using the selection as the container. It also accepts some configuration (the margin, in this case) that we can set beforehand. To learn more about this pattern you can read this blog post on Eventbrite's Engineering Blog.

searchDocs.title: Rendering a line chart​
searchDocs.content: Let's build on top of the Bar Chart tutorial by using its code structure. We load the same bundle, which has every chart:  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js"></script>   Then, we will instantiate a line chart:  const lineChart = core.line();   The shape of our data changed as well. We need to check the line chart data schema for this chart. In our case, it looks like this:  const lineData = { "data": [ { "value": 0, "name": -1, "topicName": "Vivid", "date": "2016-08-01T00:00:00-07:00" }, { "value": 3, "name": 2, "topicName": "Radiant", "date": "2016-08-01T00:00:00-07:00" }, ... ] };   Before configuring the chart, we figure out the container's size to apply it as the chart width:  const container = document.querySelector('.line-container'); const containerWidth = container.getBoundingClientRect().width;   Configuring and rendering the line chart follows an identical approach as with the bar chart:  lineChart .margin({bottom: 50}) .height(400) .width(containerWidth); lineChart.render(container, lineData);   That renders the following chart:

searchDocs.title: Adding a Tooltip​
searchDocs.content: Now that we have a line chart working, we are going to add a tooltip to allow users to check the specific values on each date. We start by instantiating a new Tooltip component:  const chartTooltip = core.tooltip();   Then we give it to the line chart:  lineChart .margin({bottom: 50}) .height(400) .width(containerWidth) .tooltip(chartTooltip); lineChart.render(container, lineData);   The chart does the rest. It shows the tooltip when the pointer enters the chart, or when the keyboard moves to a date, updates it as they move, and hides it when they leave. It draws the tooltip in its hover marker, and tells the tooltip which fields of its data to read. After the previous code, we will see a tooltip like the following:

searchDocs.title: Drawing a Legend​
searchDocs.content: Up to now, we have been working with a dataset that contains only one topic. But what happens if we have two topics? In this section, we will update our data to contain another set of entries. We add a legend component to show our users which line corresponds to which topic.  First, we make a copy of the topic we already have and change some values. We named the new topic "Radiant," and due to our default color schema, it shows as a dark green line.  Now we instantiate our new legend component:  const chartLegend = core.legend();   The same way as we needed a container for the chart, we require another for the legend:  <div class="legend-container"></div>   The legend is a component that depends on the data and in a specific data shape. We check the Legend data schema, and it needs to be:  [ { id: 1, quantity: 2, name: 'glittering' }, { id: 2, quantity: 3, name: 'luminous' } ]   As we want to show an inline legend, which doesn't show the quantity, we only need one entry per line, with its name, an id and a quantity of zero. Here is how we create that data:  // One entry per line: every point repeats its line's name and topicName const legendData = Array.from( new Map( lineData.data.map(({ topicName, name }) => [ name, { id: name, name: topicName, quantity: 0 }, ]) ).values() );   And we are ready to configure and draw the legend:  chartLegend .width(containerWidth) .height(60) .isHorizontal(true); chartLegend.render('.legend-container', legendData);   Note how we have used the container width to position the legend in the center. You can see the rest of the options of the legend component in its API reference page.  The resulting chart is:

searchDocs.title: Filtering Data with a Brush​
searchDocs.content: Our current data is not that extensive, but in theory, our line chart could render datasets of any size. This could be a problem as we could get into a position where the data points get too close, and our users can't see the details of the data. One way of fixing this is by allowing to filter data, and the way we do it visually is by using a brush chart.  In this section, we go over the process of adding a brush chart to our visualization, allowing to drag and drop a section of the data to zoom in that period.

searchDocs.title: Creating the brush chart​
searchDocs.content: Let's first instantiate the brush chart:  const chartBrush = core.brush();   We would need to add its container to the DOM:  <div class="brush-container"></div>   Now, as we did before, we are going to check the Brush Chart API and its data schema. The data needs to look like this:  [ { value: 1, date: "2011-01-06T00:00:00Z" }, { value: 2, date: "2011-01-07T00:00:00Z" } ]   So, in order to get this data shape, we will need to do some modifications to our line chart data:  const brushData = lineData.data .reduce(consolidateDatesReducer, []);   In the first reducer function, we obtain the entries by date, keeping only date and values. On the second one, we remove duplicated dates and sum up the values to have an aggregate of them. You can check the details of these functions in the final code.  Now we are ready to configure and render our brush using the usual pattern:  chartBrush .width(containerWidth) .height(100) .xAxisFormat(chartBrush.axisTimeCombinations.DAY_MONTH) .margin({top:0, bottom: 40, left: 50, right: 30}); chartBrush.render('.brush-container', brushData);   Notice that we are setting the x-axis format to a constant called DAY_MONTH within the axisTimeCombinations object. This xAxisFormat option is a way for us to select a date format that works for our data. In this case, it is the day of the month, as the default one (hours) was showing the same hour every day.  This code renders a simple Brush chart:  This chart only serves as an overview of the sum of data in our dataset. What we want to do is, when we drag and drop a section of the brush, select that portion of our dataset and re-render the line chart with it.  For that, we listen to the customBrushEnd event on the brush, that returns the period of the brush selection. We take the beginning and end of that period and filter our original data with them. Finally, we apply it to the line chart and re-render. Here is the code for it:  chartBrush .width(containerWidth) .height(100) .xAxisFormat(chartBrush.axisTimeCombinations.DAY_MONTH) .margin({ top: 0, bottom: 40, left: 50, right: 30 }) .on('customBrushEnd', ([brushStart, brushEnd]) => { if (brushStart && brushEnd) { let filteredLineData = filterData(brushStart, brushEnd); lineChart.render(container, filteredLineData); } });   This results in a data visualization where we can focus on different sections of the data, and use our tooltip to see the values on those:  Here is the filtering logic for your reference:  const isInRange = (startDate, endDate, {date}) => new Date(date) >= startDate && new Date(date) <= endDate; const filterData = (brushStart, brushEnd) => { // Copy the data let data = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(lineData)); data.data = data.data.filter(isInRange.bind(null, brushStart, brushEnd)); return data; };   You can see the full code of this tutorial in this file and the tutorial working here.

searchDocs.title: Downloading Britecharts​
searchDocs.content: To use a Britechart, we need to install the library. In this tutorial, we are going to use a simple CDN link to install it. For that, create a simple HTML file and add this script tag:  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js" type="text/javascript"></script>   The bundle has every chart, and the d3 modules they use, so the page needs no other script.  We also need to load the styling of our chart, and we do it similarly by accesing the CDN link:  <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@britecharts/core/dist/styles/bundle/britecharts.min.css" type="text/css" />

searchDocs.title: Setting up Container, Dataset and Chart​
searchDocs.content: To create a container, we add a div in the DOM with a class:  <div class="bar-container"></div>   We instantiate a new chart by calling the function bar() inside the core object in the global namespace:  const barChart = core.bar();   We need a simple dataset to render the bar chart. We can find the right format of the data by visiting the API documentation for the bar chart component. Developers need to find the data definition at the top of the page; in this case, it is a link labeled BarChartData. It looks like this:  [ { value: 1, name: 'glittering' }, { value: 1, name: 'luminous' } ]   We can extend that definition to have some more bars, for example:  const barData = [ { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 }, { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 }, { name: 'Intense', value: 4 }, { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 } ];

searchDocs.title: Configuring and Rendering the bar chart​
searchDocs.content: We only need to configure our bar chart by calling the accessors. We describe these in the bar chart API reference page. In this tutorial, we set it up as a horizontal bar chart with a height of 400px and a width of 600px:  barChart .margin({left: 100}) .isHorizontal(true) .height(400) .width(600);   Notice how we tweaked a bit the left margin in order to allow space for our left aligned labels to render.  We only need to render our configured bar chart into the container, with the data:  barChart.render('.bar-container', barData);   render takes a CSS selector, an element or a d3 selection. Calling it again with new data redraws the chart. To render a simple bar chart:    Here is all the code inside the <body> tag of our HTML file:  <div class="bar-container"></div> <script> // Instantiate bar chart const barChart = core.bar(); // Create Dataset with proper shape const barData = [ { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 }, { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 }, { name: 'Intense', value: 4 }, { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 } ]; // Configure chart barChart .margin({left: 100}) .isHorizontal(true) .height(400) .width(600); barChart.render('.bar-container', barData); </script>   In version 3 of Britecharts, the rendered charts are already responsive, so you can stretch and compress the viewport size to see the chart react.  You can check the full code of this tutorial in this file and the tutorial working here.

searchDocs.title: Summary​
searchDocs.content: In this tutorial, we have seen how to load Britecharts with a CDN link and how to draw a simple chart. We did this by checking the API Reference page for the chart and its data schema and by creating the elements needed in the HTML file.  To keep on learning more about Britecharts, you can follow our Composing Your First Data Visualization tutorial or read abbout how to install Britecharts in your project. You can also check out our Documentation Homepage and our kitchen sink to see all the available charts.  If you are excited about Britecharts, want to add more configurable properties or even create your own chart, please check our Contributing Guide. In it, we walk you through the development environment setup, running our docs and demos and creating new Pull Requests.

searchDocs.title: Applying a color palette​
searchDocs.content: Let's look at some customization options we have available for Britecharts. The first one is the color schemas and gradients. You can find some of them in our Color Palettes demo page.  To get us started with a tutorial, we are going to take our Getting Started tutorial code and create a new HTML file based on it.  We will start from the code we got at the end of that tutorial, removing the responsive part:  // Instantiate Bar Chart const barChart = core.bar(); // Create Dataset with proper shape const barData = [ { name: 'Luminous', value: 2 }, { name: 'Glittering', value: 5 }, { name: 'Intense', value: 4 }, { name: 'Radiant', value: 3 } ]; // Configure chart barChart .margin({ left: 100 }) .isHorizontal(true) .height(400) .width(600); barChart.render('.bar-container', barData);   Starting with this bar chart, we want to customize the color palette. The color schemas come with the bundle, as core.colors, so we can set the color schema of the bar chart by doing:  // Configure chart barChart .colorSchema(core.colors.colorSchemas.orange) .margin({ left: 100 }) .isHorizontal(true) .height(400) .width(600);   That renders an orange bar chart:  The different color palettes we provide in Britecharts are ubicated within the colorSchemas object. You can see their colors them in the demo page.  When we look at the palettes code, they are just an array of nine hexadecimal values. For example:  // Britecharts palette ["#6aedc7", "#39c2c9", "#ffce00", "#ffa71a", "#f866b9", "#998ce3"]   Which means that if you want to customize your charts color palette, you only need to pass an array of hexadecimal colors into the .colorSchema accessors.

searchDocs.title: Using a color gradient​
searchDocs.content: Some Britecharts use a color gradient for their lines (line, sparkline and stacked area charts) or for the body of the chart (brush).  You can find these color gradients in core.colors.colorGradients and similarly, they are an array of colors. However, in this case they are only two colors, one for the beginning and another for the end of the gradient.

searchDocs.title: Overriding default styles​
searchDocs.content: Whenever we want to change the font family, font sizes or any other styling detail of our charts, we can do so by creating CSS overrides. As an example, let's change the font of our bar chart.  We'll begin by looking for a new font in Google Fonts. I am a fan of the font Oswald, so let's add it to our tutorial by including this link tag in the header:  <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Oswald:600" rel="stylesheet">   Now, we need to set up a style override. For that, we can inspect our SVG elements with the dev tools of our browser. In this case, we see that the font-family attribute is set by the .britechart class. To override it, we need to add a style tag after the link that loads the default britecharts styling and inside the tag, include following code:  <style> .britechart, .tick text { font-family: 'Oswald', sans-serif; } </style>   This CSS code will override the font-family definition for both the whole chart and the specific tick text of our axes. If we also change the color schema to the red palette, we get this chart:  We could follow the same steps to style most of Britechart's styling. One caveat is that, given that Britecharts is an SVG based library, the styling of SVG elements is sometimes different. In those cases, check out this SVG styling guide to make sure you are updating the right properties.

searchDocs.title: Summary​
searchDocs.content: In this tutorial, you saw how you can use Britecharts' color helper to apply color palettes and color gradients to your charts. You also saw you can customize all the elments by using CSS style overrides. You can see the tutorial code working here.  To learn more, you can follow our Composing Your First Data Visualization tutorial. You can also check out our Documentation Homepage and our kitchen sink to see all the available charts.
